Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: IDENTIFICATION OF A STRUCTURALLY AND EVOLUTIONARILY CONSERVED 3'→5' PROOFREADING EXONUCLEASE DOMAIN IN THE LARGE L PROTEIN OF HANTAVIRUSES- EMERGING HUMAN PATHOGENS
papers.abstract: The proofreading 3′→5′ exonuclease not only represents a crucial class of enzymes responsible for maintaining genome integrity across diverse groups of organisms, but also plays a critical role in ensuring replication fidelity. In the non-segmented, positive-strand bat-borne RNA viruses like Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronaviruses (SARS-CoVs and MERS-CoV), it is found along with the methyltransferase (MTase) gene of the non-structural protein 14 (NSP14). In contrast, in the non-segmented, but negative-strand bat-borne RNA viruses such as Marburg, Ebola and Nipah viruses, it has been identified together with a novel type of capping enzyme, viz. guanosine diphosphate polyribonucleotidyltransferase (PRNTase). Hantaviruses, one of the fatal and emerging human pathogens in recent times, belong to segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses and are primarily rodent-borne. Currently, no universally approved vaccine or antiviral therapy exists for all hantavirus infections. The presence of a proofreading (PR) exonuclease domain has not been reported in hantaviruses until now. Interestingly, a putative PR exonuclease domain has been identified for the first time in these viruses within the large L protein, preceding the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). The newly identified domain belongs to the DEDD superfamily, but exhibits a distinct structural deviation, notably the replacement of the first catalytic triad -DxE- in the Old World hantaviruses with an -NxE- motif in most of the New World hantaviruses, and the use of an invariant tyrosine instead of histidine at the proton acceptor site. This feature closely resembles the DEDD superfamily of PR exonucleases reported in bacterial DNA polymerases I and II and in the DNA-dependent DNA polymerases of DNA viruses. To the best of my knowledge, this study provides the first evidence for the presence of a typical DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease domain in hantaviruses, and thus, expanding our understanding of the structure and catalytic mechanism of 3′→5′ PR exonucleases in segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses and further presenting a novel structural target for the development of universally effective antiviral therapies against fatal hantavirus infections.

papers.title: Development of a Rapid RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b Assay for Dual Detection of Hantaan Virus and Seoul Virus.
papers.abstract: Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the primary causative agents of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), presenting a persistent challenge to global public health. Prompt and precise diagnostic tools are essential for clinical investigation and the containment of HFRS outbreaks. Leveraging the programmable precision of CRISPR/Cas12b system, which has significantly advanced the field of molecular diagnostics, we developed a rapid, high-sensitivity assay for the dual detection of HTNV and SEOV. Each virus was detected in a separate, target-specific single-tube reaction. The assay combines recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with CRISPR/Cas12b-mediated fluorescence detection and uses virus-specific sgRNAs and RPA primers targeting conserved genomic regions. Using recombinant plasmid standards, both targets were detected at 1×101 copies/test in three technical replicates; this is a preliminary analytical detection threshold and does not incorporate extraction losses or matrix-associated inhibition. No cross-reactivity was observed within the evaluated four-organism non-target panel. In a preliminary feasibility assessment, all nine RT-qPCR-positive rodent samples (seven HTNV and two SEOV) were positive by the RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b assay, indicating complete positive agreement in this all-positive sample set. Because no negative samples were included, negative agreement, diagnostic specificity, false-positive rate, and overall clinical diagnostic accuracy could not be assessed. These results support further development of the assay as a potential screening tool; larger studies using well-characterized positive and negative clinical or field specimens are required.

analysis_zh.methods: 作者将重组酶聚合酶扩增(RPA)与CRISPR/Cas12b介导的荧光检测相结合,使用针对保守区域的病毒特异性sgRNA和引物;通过重组质粒标准评估分析灵敏度,并使用四种非目标生物的面板评估特异性;在九个RT‐qPCR阳性的啮齿动物样本(七例HTNV,二例SEOV)中测试可行性。
analysis_zh.results: 该检测在三次重复中每次检测限为10拷贝,未出现对非目标面板的交叉反应,并在九个啮齿动物样本中与RT‐qPCR实现100 %阳性一致率;阴性一致率和整体诊断准确性未能评估。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些结果支持进一步开发RPA‐CRISPR/Cas12b检测,作为针对HTNV和SEOV的快速高灵敏度筛查工具,需待更大规模的验证研究。
analysis_zh.limitations: 检测限未考虑提取损失或基质抑制,且研究缺乏阴性样本,导致无法评估特异性、假阳性率及整体临床准确性;结论基于仅有摘要的报告。

papers.title: Computational Evaluation of a Novel Nitrothiophene-Derived Schiff Base Ligand Against Breast Cancer-Associated Proteins and Andes Hantavirus Nucleoprotein: Molecular Docking and ADMET Analysis
papers.abstract: The identification of small molecules capable of interacting with multiple therapeutically relevant protein targets is an important strategy in early-stage drug discovery. In the present study, the Schiff base ligand ((N1E,N8E)-N1,N8-bis((5-nitrothiophen-2-yl)methylene)naphthalene-1,8-diamine; N1) was computationally evaluated against a panel of representative disease-associated proteins to investigate its target-binding profile. The primary focus was the assessment of N1 against breast cancer-associated receptor kinases, including EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K, which play central roles in oncogenic signaling pathways. In addition, the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein was included as an exploratory antiviral target to examine the broader target recognition capability of the ligand rather than to propose a common therapeutic mechanism. Molecular docking studies were performed using AutoDock Vina with experimentally determined protein structures obtained from the Protein Data Bank. N1 demonstrated favorable binding affinities toward all investigated breast cancer targets, with docking scores of −8.708 kcal/mol for EGFR, −8.836 kcal/mol for HER2, −8.906 kcal/mol for VEGFR2, and −9.066 kcal/mol for PI3K. The ligand also exhibited a docking score of −8.8 kcal/mol against the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein. Interaction analysis revealed multiple stabilizing hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, electrostatic interactions, and π-mediated interactions within the respective binding pockets.Drug-likeness assessment indicated compliance with Lipinski's and Ghose's rules, while ADMET prediction suggested favorable absorption and membrane permeability. Nevertheless, the predicted risks of hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, and mutagenicity indicate that further structural optimization and experimental validation are required. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of N1 as a promising scaffold for breast cancer-associated kinase inhibition while providing preliminary evidence of its broader protein-binding capability across biologically distinct targets.

Keywords: Breast cancer, Hantavirus, Molecular docking, Drug-likeness, ADMET, Schiff base Cite This Article: Temitayo O. Aiyelabola, Sayantan Pradhan, and Takashiro Akitsu, “Computational Evaluation of a Novel Nitrothiophene-Derived Schiff Base Ligand Against Breast Cancer-Associated Proteins and Andes Hantavirus Nucleoprotein: Molecular Docking and ADMET Analysis.” Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry, vol. 14, no. 1 (2026): 1-14. doi: 10.12691/jpbpc-14-1-1. 1. Introduction Cancer and viral infections remain among the most serious global health challenges due to their high mortality rates, rapid disease progression, and limited availability of effective therapeutic agents [1,2]. Among different malignancies, breast cancer is one of the most frequently diagnosed cancers and represents a leading cause of cancer-related death among women worldwide [3]. The development and progression of breast cancer are closely associated with abnormal activation of receptor tyrosine kinases and intracellular signaling proteins, particularly Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR), Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2), Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Receptor 2 (VEGFR2), and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) [4,5,6]. These signaling proteins regulate essential cellular processes such as proliferation, angiogenesis, migration, metastasis, survival, and apoptosis. Overexpression or mutation of these targets has been strongly linked with aggressive tumor 2 Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry progression and poor clinical prognosis [7]. EGFR and HER2 activation initiates downstream signaling cascades, including the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways, which contribute to uncontrolled cancer cell proliferation, enhanced survival, and metastatic progression (Figure 1) [8,9]. VEGFR2 plays a crucial role in tumor angiogenesis by stimulating endothelial cell migration and vascular formation necessary for tumor growth and metastasis [10]. PI3K, a central component of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, regulates cellular growth, proliferation, metabolism, and survival and is frequently dysregulated in breast cancer [11]. Collectively, EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K represent interconnected signaling proteins that regulate complementary aspects of breast cancer progression, including cell proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, and metastasis. Since these proteins belong to functionally linked oncogenic signaling networks, their simultaneous computational evaluation provides an opportunity to investigate whether a single chemical scaffold can potentially interact with multiple biologically relevant targets involved in breast cancer. It should be noted that the present study aims to explore the binding characteristics of N1 toward these proteins through molecular docking and does not imply experimentally validated inhibition of these signaling pathways. Therefore, EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K were selected as representative breast cancer-associated targets for an exploratory computational target-profiling study (Figure 1) [8,9,10,11]. In addition to cancer, viral infections caused by emerging and re-emerging viruses continue to pose major public health concerns worldwide. Andes hantavirus, a member of the Hantaviridae family, is responsible for hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), a severe respiratory disease associated with high fatality rates [12]. The viral nucleoprotein (N protein) plays an essential role in viral RNA encapsidation, ribonucleoprotein complex formation, genome replication, and viral assembly, making it a biologically relevant target for antiviral drug discovery (Figure 2) [13]. Unlike viral enzymes, the nucleoprotein does not possess catalytic activity; instead, its RNA-binding region is responsible for recognizing and stabilizing viral genomic RNA during ribonucleoprotein assembly. Accordingly, the molecular docking analysis in the present study focused on this functionally important RNA-binding region to evaluate the potential molecular recognition of N1. Binding at this site may theoretically interfere with RNA recognition or ribonucleoprotein assembly; however, such effects remain computational hypotheses that require experimental validation [13,14]. The inclusion of the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein was intended as an exploratory assessment of the binding versatility of the N1 scaffold against a structurally unrelated viral target rather than to propose a unified therapeutic strategy linking breast cancer and hantavirus infection. Despite the severe pathogenicity associated with hantavirus infections, currently available antiviral therapies remain limited, emphasizing the continuing need to identify new antiviral scaffolds for future investigation [14]. In the present work, we report the synthesis and computational evaluation of a novel nitrothiophene- derived Schiff base ligand (N1). The primary objective of this study was to investigate its interaction with multiple breast cancer-associated kinase targets, including EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K, which collectively regulate tumor proliferation, survival, and angiogenesis. As an exploratory extension of this computational investigation, the ligand was also docked against the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein to assess whether this chemical scaffold exhibits potential binding capability toward a structurally unrelated viral protein involved in RNA encapsidation. This exploratory comparison should not be interpreted as evidence of a unified therapeutic strategy but rather as an initial computational assessment of the molecular recognition properties of N1 across biologically distinct protein targets. The ligand (N1E,N8E)-N1,N8-bis((5- nitrothiophen-2-yl)methylene)naphthalene-1,8-diamine, and its in silico activities are reported here for the first time. Figure 1. The figure illustrates the proposed mechanism of action of the investigated ligand against major breast cancer-associated signaling proteins, including EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K. Activation of EGFR and HER2 normally initiates downstream signaling cascades such as the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways, which promote cancer cell proliferation, survival, and metastasis. VEGFR2 activation stimulates angiogenic signaling pathways responsible for tumor vascularization and endothelial cell migration. In the proposed mechanism, inhibition of these receptors suppresses phosphorylation-mediated signaling events, thereby reducing tumor growth, angiogenesis, and metastatic progression. PI3K inhibition further decreases AKT/mTOR signaling, leading to apoptosis induction and suppression of cancer cell survival. Overall, the figure demonstrates the multi-target inhibitory action of the ligand against critical pathways involved in breast cancer progression Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry 3 Figure 2. The figure represents the life cycle of Andes hantavirus and the proposed antiviral mechanism of the investigated compound targeting the viral nucleoprotein (N protein). The hantavirus initially enters the host cell through receptor-mediated endocytosis, followed by viral uncoating and release of ribonucleoprotein complexes into the cytoplasm. Viral RNA transcription and replication are subsequently carried out by the viral RNA- dependent RNA polymerase, leading to synthesis of viral proteins and assembly of new virions. The proposed ligand is suggested to bind within the RNA-binding region of the hantavirus nucleoprotein, thereby interfering with viral RNA encapsidation and ribonucleoprotein complex formation. This inhibition may suppress viral replication, reduce formation of mature viral particles, and prevent further viral dissemination within host cells. The overall antiviral outcome includes inhibition of viral replication, reduction of viral load, and prevention of hantavirus propagation 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Synthesis: Material All starting materials and solvents used were purchased from Aldrich and Fluka and were used without further purification. Melting points were determined in an open capillary tube on a Gallenkamp (Variable heater) melting point apparatus. NMR spectrum (1H) was recorded on an analysis X-685 benchtop NMR spectrophotometer at 60 MHz DMSO-d6 with TMS as internal standard, at the central science laboratory, Covenant University, Ota. The infrared spectra of all synthesized products were obtained using Agilent Cary 630 FTIR. The electronic spectra, of all the compounds, were obtained in solution, in the wavelength range 400-1000 nm using 1800 Shimadzu ultra-violet spectrophotometer. Both were carried out at the central science laboratory, Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife. 2.2. Synthesis; Experimental An ethanolic solution of 1,8-diaminonaphthalene (0.83 g, 5.00 mmol) was introduced to a solution of 5-nitro-2- carboxaldehyde (1.62 g, 10.0 mmol) in absolute ethanol (25 mL) supplemented with glacial acetic acid (3 drops) as a catalyst. The reaction mixture was subjected to reflux conditions for 4 hours under atmospheric pressure. Following thermal treatment, the reaction vessel was allowed to equilibrate to ambient temperature, after which the volatile organic solvent was removed via rotary evaporation under reduced pressure until precipitation of a solid product occurred. The crude material was subsequently triturated with cold ethanol and subjected to recrystallization from a chloroform/ethanol solvent mixture (volume ratio 30:70). A deep orange-colored solid was obtained, collected by vacuum filtration, and dried under reduced pressure at 60°C until constant mass was achieved, yielding N1 as the isolated product. The compound demonstrated appreciable solubility in chloroform, ethanol, and methanol. The schematic representation for the preparation of N1 is given in Scheme 1. Yield: 1.49 g, 68.78%; m.p: 165 ̊C - 166 ̊C (d); IR (cm−1): 1608 ν(C=C), 1587 ν(C=N), 1423 ν(C=C, thiophene aromatic ring) 1490 and 1326 ν(NO2), UV-Vis (nm): 299; 1 H NMR (60 MHz): DMSO-d6 δ 7.95 (s, 1H), 7.21, 7.04 (d, 6H), 6.64, 6.55 (d, 2H). Scheme 1. Schematic representation of the synthesis pathway of the novel Schiff base ligand N1, (N1E,N8E)-N1,N8-bis((5-nitrothiophen-2- yl)methylene)naphthalene-1,8-diamine formed through the condensation reaction between 5-nitrothiophene-2-carbaldehyde and naphthalene-1,8- diamine. The figure also illustrates the optimized three-dimensional molecular structure of the synthesized compound 2.3. Retrieval of Protein Structures The three-dimensional crystal structures of the selected 4 Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry therapeutic targets associated with breast cancer and viral infection were retrieved from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). The protein structures used in this study included epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR, PDB ID: 1M17, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2, PDB ID: 3PP0), vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2, PDB ID: 1YWN), phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K, PDB ID: 4JPS), and Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein (PDB ID: 5E04 ). The biologically relevant protein chain (Chain A) was selected for all docking studies. These structures were chosen based on their high crystallographic resolution and the presence of co- crystallized ligands within the active site, allowing accurate definition of the ligand-binding pocket for molecular docking. 2.4. Protein Preparation Protein preparation was performed using AutoDock Tools. Prior to docking, all crystallographic water molecules, co-crystallized ligands, and non-essential heteroatoms were removed while preserving the protein backbone and active-site residues. Polar hydrogen atoms were subsequently added, and Kollman united-atom partial charges were assigned to the protein structures. The prepared receptors were saved in PDBQT format for docking calculations [19]. 2.5. Ligand Preparation The chemical structure of the synthesized ligand was generated using ChemDraw Professional 12.0 and converted into a three-dimensional structure using Avogadro . Geometry optimization was carried out using the MMFF94 force field until convergence to obtain a minimum-energy conformation. Hydrogen atoms were added, appropriate protonation corresponding to physiological pH (approximately 7.4) was assigned, and Gasteiger partial atomic charges were calculated using AutoDock Tools. The optimized ligand was finally converted into PDBQT format for molecular docking [20,21]. 2.6. Molecular Docking Molecular docking studies were performed using AutoDock Vina (version 1.2.7) to evaluate the binding affinity and binding mode of the ligand against the selected protein targets. The docking grid was centered on the active-site region defined by the co-crystallized ligand in each receptor structure. A grid box of 25 × 25 × 25 Å with a grid spacing of 1.0 Å was employed to adequately encompass the entire binding pocket. Docking calculations were carried out using an exhaustiveness value of 8, and 10 binding poses were generated for each protein-ligand complex. The resulting docking conformations were ranked according to their predicted binding free energies (kcal/mol). The optimal binding pose for each complex was selected based on the lowest binding free energy together with a favorable binding orientation and the formation of key interactions with biologically relevant active-site residues identified from the corresponding crystal structures and supported by previous literature [22,23]. 2.7. Drug-Likeness Evaluation The drug-likeness properties of N1 were evaluated using widely accepted computational pharmacokinetic filters, including Lipinski’s Rule of Five and Ghose’s filter, to assess its suitability as a potential orally active therapeutic agent. Physicochemical parameters such as molecular weight, hydrogen bond acceptors, hydrogen bond donors, partition coefficient (logP), molar refractivity, and total number of atoms were calculated to determine the drug-like behavior and oral bioavailability of the compound [24,25]. Lipinski’s Rule of Five was applied based on the criteria of molecular weight below 500 Da, hydrogen bond acceptors fewer than 10, hydrogen bond donors fewer than 5, and logP value below 5, which are considered favorable for oral drug candidates [24]. In addition, Ghose’s filter was employed to further evaluate the compound by considering acceptable ranges of molecular weight, lipophilicity, molar refractivity, and atom count commonly associated with biologically active molecules [25]. All calculations and predictions were performed using an online ADMET and drug-likeness prediction platform. The obtained parameters were analyzed to determine the compliance of N1 with established drug- likeness criteria 2.8. full_text_sections.full_text: Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry, 2026, Vol. 14, No. 1, 1-14 Available online at http://pubs.sciepub.com/jpbpc/14/1/1 Published by Science and Education Publishing DOI:10.12691/jpbpc-14-1-1 Computational Evaluation of a Novel Nitrothiophene- Derived Schiff Base Ligand Against Breast Cancer-Associated Proteins and Andes Hantavirus Nucleoprotein: Molecular Docking and ADMET Analysis Temitayo O. Aiyelabola1,*, Sayantan Pradhan2,*, Takashiro Akitsu3 1Department of Chemistry, Faculty of Science, Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife, Osun State, Nigeria 2Chemical Science Division, Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics, Kolkata, West Bengal, India 3Department of Chemistry, Faculty of Science, Tokyo University of Science, 1-3 Kagurazaka, Shinjuku-ku, Tokyo 162-8601, Japan *Corresponding author: Received September 07, 2026; Revised October 09, 2026; Accepted October 16, 2026 Abstract The identification of small molecules capable of interacting with multiple therapeutically relevant protein targets is an important strategy in early-stage drug discovery. In the present study, the Schiff base ligand ((N1E,N8E)-N1,N8-bis((5-nitrothiophen-2-yl)methylene)naphthalene-1,8-diamine; N1) was computationally evaluated against a panel of representative disease-associated proteins to investigate its target-binding profile. The primary focus was the assessment of N1 against breast cancer-associated receptor kinases, including EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K, which play central roles in oncogenic signaling pathways. In addition, the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein was included as an exploratory antiviral target to examine the broader target recognition capability of the ligand rather than to propose a common therapeutic mechanism. Molecular docking studies were performed using AutoDock Vina with experimentally determined protein structures obtained from the Protein Data Bank. N1 demonstrated favorable binding affinities toward all investigated breast cancer targets, with docking scores of −8.708 kcal/mol for EGFR, −8.836 kcal/mol for HER2, −8.906 kcal/mol for VEGFR2, and −9.066 kcal/mol for PI3K. The ligand also exhibited a docking score of −8.8 kcal/mol against the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein. Interaction analysis revealed multiple stabilizing hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, electrostatic interactions, and π-mediated interactions within the respective binding pockets.Drug-likeness assessment indicated compliance with Lipinski's and Ghose's rules, while ADMET prediction suggested favorable absorption and membrane permeability. Nevertheless, the predicted risks of hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, and mutagenicity indicate that further structural optimization and experimental validation are required. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of N1 as a promising scaffold for breast cancer-associated kinase inhibition while providing preliminary evidence of its broader protein-binding capability across biologically distinct targets. Accordingly, the molecular docking analysis in the present study focused on this functionally important RNA-binding region to evaluate the potential molecular recognition of N1. Binding at this site may theoretically interfere with RNA recognition or ribonucleoprotein assembly; however, such effects remain computational hypotheses that require experimental validation [13,14]. The inclusion of the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein was intended as an exploratory assessment of the binding versatility of the N1 scaffold against a structurally unrelated viral target rather than to propose a unified therapeutic strategy linking breast cancer and hantavirus infection. analysis.methods: The Schiff base ligand N1 was evaluated by molecular docking using AutoDock Vina with protein structures from the Protein Data Bank, targeting breast‑cancer kinases (EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, PI3K) and the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein.
analysis.results: N1 achieved docking scores of –8.708 to –9.066 kcal/mol for the four kinases and –8.8 kcal/mol for the viral nucleoprotein; interaction analysis showed hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic, electrostatic and π‑mediated contacts; drug‑likeness met Lipinski and Ghose criteria and ADMET predicted good absorption, yet in silico alerts indicated possible hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity and mutagenicity.
analysis.contribution: The authors propose N1 as a promising scaffold for multi‑kinase inhibition in breast cancer and as a lead for broader protein‑binding applications, including antiviral exploration.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Identifying small molecules that can bind multiple therapeutic targets is crucial for early drug discovery. Methods: The Schiff base ligand N1 was docked (AutoDock Vina) against breast‑cancer kinases and Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein using PDB structures. Results: N1 showed docking scores of –8.708 to –9.066 kcal/mol for EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, PI3K and –8.8 kcal/mol for the viral protein, with stabilizing interactions; it met drug‑likeness rules and showed favorable ADMET but predicted hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity and mutagenicity. Contribution: The study suggests N1 as a promising multi‑kinase scaffold and a potential antiviral lead. Limitations: Findings are solely in silico with no experimental validation and indicate toxicity concerns requiring optimization.

papers.title: From Systemic Inflammation to Calcium Leak: The RyR2 Hypothesis of Reversible Myocardial Dysfunction in Andes Virus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome
papers.abstract: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by Andes virus is a severe zoonotic disease characterized by a paradoxical cardiac phenotype: profound myocardial dysfunction that is frequently reversible in survivors and occurs without extensive structural damage. The mechanisms linking systemic inflammation to this reversible dysfunction remain unknown. This review examines the hypothesis that inflammatory signaling converges on the cardiac ryanodine receptor (RyR2), a major intracellular Ca2+-release channel, through post-translational modifications, generating reversible myocardial dysfunction in HCPS. In severe disease, elevated IL-6, reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, and nitrosative stress activate pathways that in experimental models converge on RyR2 through CaMKII-dependent phosphorylation at Ser2814, oxidative modification of cysteine residues, and S-nitrosylation, each destabilizing the channel and promoting diastolic Ca2+ leak. The resulting increase in spontaneous Ca2+ release reduces SR Ca2+ content, impairs contractility, and predisposes to arrhythmias. This framework identifies RyR2 as a plausible mechanistic hub for the reversible cardiac phenotype. Therapeutic implications are discussed, emphasizing the timing of interventions and the potential of rycals, drugs that stabilize the closed state of RyR2 and prevent diastolic Ca2+ leak, as an emerging strategy. This model provides a testable hypothesis for a disease that currently lacks specific treatment.

analysis.background: HCPS caused by Andes virus shows profound but often reversible myocardial dysfunction without major structural damage, prompting investigation. (A1)
analysis.main_directions: The review hypothesizes that systemic inflammation targets cardiac RyR2 via IL‑6‑driven ROS/RNS, CaMKII phosphorylation, oxidative cysteine modification and S‑nitrosylation, causing diastolic Ca²⁺ leak, contractile loss and arrhythmia, and considers RyR2‑stabilizing rycals as therapy. (A3,A4,A5,A7)
analysis.current_state: Experimental data link elevated IL‑6, oxidative stress and CaMKII activation to RyR2 destabilization, supporting RyR2 as a mechanistic hub for reversible dysfunction. (A4,A6)
analysis.gaps: The precise causal chain from patient inflammation to RyR2 modification remains unproven, and clinical data on RyR2‑targeted interventions are lacking. (A2)
analysis.future_research: Testing RyR2‑stabilizing compounds in HCPS models, measuring RyR2 post‑translational marks in patients, and timing studies of anti‑inflammatory versus rycal therapy are recommended. (A7,A8)

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes‑virus HCPS causes reversible myocardial dysfunction without structural damage (A1). Main directions: Inflammation may modify RyR2 via IL‑6‑driven ROS/RNS, CaMKII phosphorylation, oxidative and nitrosylation changes, leading to Ca²⁺ leak and arrhythmia; rycals are proposed as therapy (A3,A4,A5,A7). Current state: Experimental models support RyR2 as a hub linking cytokine‑induced oxidative stress to contractile impairment (A4,A6). Gaps: Direct patient evidence for RyR2 modification and efficacy of RyR2‑targeted drugs is missing (A2). Future research: Validate RyR2 modifications in patients, test rycals in animal and clinical studies, and define optimal timing of anti‑inflammatory versus RyR2‑stabilizing interventions (A7,A8).

papers.title: Hantaviral therapeutics: life cycle targets and chemotherapeutic interventions
papers.abstract: Orthohantaviruses represent a persistent global health threat, being responsible for life-threatening diseases such as Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS). Despite high case fatality rates and recent outbreaks, there are currently no universally licensed antivirals or vaccines. Clinical management remains heavily reliant on supportive care and repurposed drugs, which often exhibit limited efficacy and dose-limiting toxicities. This review examines rational drug design strategies targeting critical steps in the viral life cycle, specifically Gn/Gc-mediated cellular entry and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp)-driven genome replication. We evaluate the current landscape of viral inhibitors, including peptidomimetics, nucleoside analogues, and naturally derived compounds. To accelerate the discovery of novel treatments, we advocate for the integration of modern in silico screening to evaluate extensive chemical and natural product libraries. These broad compound collections offer a structurally diverse and largely untapped reservoir for antiviral development. Ultimately, expanding preclinical testing to include globally neglected variants will be essential to develop broad-spectrum hantaviral therapeutics capable of mitigating future epidemic threats.
papers.journal: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology

Infection begins when the viral Gn protein docks onto host surface receptors, using integrin and protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) (Gavrilovskaya et al., 1999; Jangra et al., 2018). Once internalized via endocytosis, a drop in endosomal pH forces the viral envelope to fuse with the host membrane, releasing the genome into the cytoplasm. The viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) starts both transcription and genome replication, before structural proteins and newly synthesized RNA assemble at the Golgi complex or plasma membrane prior to budding out as mature infectious virions (see Figure 1) (Hussein et al., 2011; Hepojoki et al., 2012; Vaheri et al., 2013b; Bradfute et al., 2024). Current orthohantavirus management relies on supportive care and repurposed drugs with limited efficacy. To overcome this public health issue, this review presents existing treatment strategies and advocates for modern in silico approaches like molecular docking. Specifically, we highlight the potential of rational drug design, encouraging the systematic virtual screening of diverse chemical and natural product libraries to discover accessible, broad-spectrum hantaviral treatments. Viral entry and fusion inhibitors One of the most promising strategies to inhibit hantaviral entry into host cells is the use of cyclic peptides. With the help of a phage library, where peptide libraries are displayed on the surfaces of filamentous bacteriophages, Larson et al. (2005) identified cyclic nonapeptides that bind the b3-integrin receptor, which pathogenic orthohantaviruses like Sin Nombre virus (SNV), Hantaan virus (HTNV), Seoul virus (SEOV), and Puumala virus (PUUV) bind for viral entry into human endothelial cells. Kocabiyik et al. 10.3389/fcimb.2026.1972830 Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology frontiersin.org 02 potency when presented by phage (IC50 = 2.7 x 108 particles/μL) (Larson et al., 2005). This peptide was further refined to its minimal functional unit required through alanine substitution and deletion scanning to the cyclic pentapeptide cyclo-[CPFVC] (Hall et al., 2007). However, because free monovalent peptides were less effec- tive than those presented on phage, subsequent research (Hall et al., 2008) shifted towards presenting peptides in a multivalent format on nanoparticles and targeting the orthohantavirus glycoproteins directly rather than the host b3-integrin receptor. The three most potent binders of the virion were selected and attached to 100 nm nanoparticles to create a multivalent inhibitor. When the peptide CLVRNLAWC was presented on a nanoparticle at a 4:1 ratio, its inhibition of SNV jumped from 9% (as a free peptide) to 32.5%. However, the peptide CQATTARNC achieved an even higher efficacy, with inhibition surpassing 50% when the nanoparticle- to-virus ratio was increased to 20:1 (Hall et al., 2008). Building on these strategies, the research was expanded to Andes virus (ANDV). Using a similar approach, Hall et al. (2009) eluted the peptide library from purified ANDV particles using monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) against the Gn and Gc glycoproteins. A major finding in this study was the combined use of peptides that targeted different Gn- and Gc-specific sequences resulted in synergistic inhibition (anti-Gc/Gn peptides CMQSAAAHC and CTVGPTRSC) of infec- tion that was significantly more powerful than single-peptide treatments, emphasizing the benefit of targeting multiple viral epitopes (Hall et al., 2009). Lastly, to search for peptidomimetic molecules to block SNV infection, Hall et al. (2010) used the 3D structure of the previously refined pentapeptide cyclo-[CPFVC], in a ligand-based virtual screening approach to evaluate over 600,000 small molecules. This transition from biological peptides to drug- like peptidomimetics identified compounds such as G319–0078 and 8012-0652, which were 2,000 times more potent than the original cyclic peptides. These molecules demonstrated high-affinity inhibi- tion in the nanomolar range in vitro (EC50 values between 1.3 - 2.5 nM) (Hall et al., 2010), successfully evolving the initial lead into a highly potent preclinical candidate warranting further in vivo evaluation. Another distinct strategy to prevent infection focuses on dis- rupting the viral membrane fusion process. Because the orthohantavirus Gc glycoprotein functions as a class II fusion protein, completing membrane fusion requires a major structural relocation of Domain III (DIII) to achieve the post-fusion state (Barriga et al., 2016; Arata-Salas et al., 2026). Exploiting this mechanical vulnerability, Barriga et al. (2016) demonstrated that viral entry can be successfully blocked using recombinant fragments and synthetic peptides derived from the Gc DIII and stem region. These fragments allow initial Gc trimerization to proceed but ultimately inhibit the pathway by preventing membrane hemifusion and fusion pore formation (Barriga et al., 2016). The recombinant DIII fragment inhibited ANDV fusion by around 70% at 25 μM and demonstrated cross-reactivity by reducing PUUV-mediated fusion by 50%. Even greater potency was observed with the R2 peptide, derived from the C-terminal part of the Gc stem region, which inhibited ANDV fusion by up to 95% in vitro (Barriga et al., 2016). Although efficacy dropped to a 70% cross-reduction (at 20 μM) against PUUV-mediated fusion (Barriga et al., 2016) due to its high genetic divergence between the two viruses, it still demonstrates significant cross-protective potential. Another very potent cell-entry inhibitor is Griffithsin (GRFT), an algae-derived lectin that has demonstrated high efficacy against several enveloped viruses such as coronaviruses, retroviruses, lentiviruses, flaviviruses, hepaciviruses, paramyxoviruses, and her- pesviruses, with the notable exclusion of gamma- and delta-retro- viruses. Interestingly, GRFT is also effective against the non- enveloped human papillomavirus (HPV), where it acts during a late step in the viral entry process rather than during initial attachment (O’Keefe et al., 2010; Lusvarghi and Bewley, 2016). In vivo administration of GRFT demonstrated clear therapeutic effi- cacy, significantly mitigating disease severity and reducing mortality in lethal SARS-CoV infection models (O’Keefe et al., 2010). Highlighting its strong translational potential, GRFT has also advanced to phase I clinical trials against human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1) infections (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifiers: NCT04032717, NCT02875119). In addition to potent inhibition of ANDV entry (Shrivastava-Ranjan et al., 2020), found that a synthetic trimeric variant (3mGRFT) possessing nine oligosaccha- ride-binding sites demonstrated even greater in vitro potency against ANDV and SNV. However, in contrast to its post-infection efficacy seen in other viral models (Lusvarghi and Bewley, 2016), the authors observed that GRFT lacked potent inhibitory activity against ANDV post-infection. While GRFT showed in vitro effec- tivity against New World hantaviruses (Shrivastava-Ranjan et al., 2020), the lectin inhibited HTNV in vivo and provided partial protection in suckling mice infected with HTNV (Zhao et al., 2022). Moreover, GRFT can be produced on a large scale and can be easily purified, highlighting its potential as an antiviral candidate for further preclinical testing against orthohantaviruses (Zhao et al., 2022). Exploring natural host defense proteins, bovine lactoferrin (LF) has demonstrated significant efficacy as a viral inhibitor against SEOV. LF prevents initial viral adsorption and adhesion, likely by interacting with cellular glycosaminoglycans such as heparin, or by sterically hindering the virus from binding to host b-integrin and lectin receptors (Murphy et al., 2000, 2001). Importantly, LF has no antiviral effect once the virus entered the host cell. In vivo, prophylactic administration of LF one day prior to orthohantavirus inoculation improved survival rates in mice up to 70% (at 160 mg/ kg), with a double-administration regimen enhancing survival to over 94%. Furthermore, when prophylactic LF treatment was combined with subsequent ribavirin administration, the two agents functioned synergistically, profoundly reducing viral shed- ding and completely inhibiting viral protein expression (Murphy et al., 2000, 2001). Discovered through a high-throughput screening of over 2,300 approved drugs and traditional Chinese medicines, cepharanthine (CEP), which is a compound isolated from Stephania cephalantha Hayata, has emerged as a highly potent viral entry and membrane fusion inhibitor. In vitro, CEP inhibited HTNV pseudovirus (EC50 value of 0.9 μM) and reduced viral nucleic acid copies by 73% at 20 μM. In vivo, administering CEP to Balb/c mice five hours post- infection significantly reduced infection by 93% (at 90 mg/kg/day) and 94% (at 180 mg/kg/day). Given its established safety profile, Kocabiyik et al. 10.3389/fcimb.2026.1972830 Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology frontiersin.org 03 CEP represents a high-priority candidate for repurposing and advancement into human clinical trials against orthohantaviruses (Wen et al., 2022). Viral replication and polymerase inhibitors Ribavirin (1-b- D-ribofuranosyl-1H-1,2,4-triazole-3- carboxamide; RBV), a synthetic guanosine nucleoside analogue, serves as the historical benchmark for anti-hantaviral therapy (Sidwell et al., 1972). Once it is transported into host cells, RBV is rapidly phosphorylated into metabolites such as RBV-5’-mono- phosphate (RBV-MP) and RBV-5’-triphosphate (RBV-TP). While RBV-MP inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH), resulting in a decrease in intracellular GTP levels, RBV-TP selectively interacts with the viral RdRp as its primary mechanism of action (Severson et al., 2003; Sun et al., 2007). The incorporation of RBV leads to accumulation of genomic errors, and thus to dramatic loss of virus viability (“error catastrophe”) (Severson et al., 2003; Chung et al., 2007). Preclinical evaluation confirmed that early RBV administration reduces viral loads and prevents severe disease in suckling mouse models infected with Hantaan virus (HTNV) and hamster models infected with Andes virus (ANDV) (Huggins et al., 1986; Ogg et al., 2013). Clinically, intravenous RBV demonstrated efficacy in a double-blind, placebo- controlled trial of 242 patients with HTNV-induced HFRS, signif- icantly reducing hemorrhagic and overall mortality (Huggins et al., 1991). However, efficacy varies significantly across strains and clinical syndromes. In the context of HCPS caused by Andes virus (ANDV), intervention with RBV eliminated mortality com- pared to a 35% historical case-fatality rate and reduced the inci- dence of the severe cardiopulmonary phase from 84% to 57% (Strella et al., 2025). Conversely, in a larger placebo-controlled, double-blinded trial evaluating intravenous RBV for HCPS, the drug failed to demonstrate overall therapeutic efficacy, revealing no significant difference in survival (70% with RBV vs. 62% with placebo), nor in necessity of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) between groups (Mertz et al., 2004). Trials in HFRS caused by Puumala virus (PUUV) also showed insufficient efficacy and safety of intravenous RBV, likely due to delayed drug administra- tion and weaker correlation between viral load and disease severity compared to HTNV infection (Malinin and Platonov, 2017). Despite its status as an established treatment for HFRS, the clinical utility of RBV is constrained by dose-limiting toxicities, most notably reversible hemolytic anemia, reported in 71% of recipients (Chapman et al., 1999; Jonsson et al., 2010). Furthermore, the lack of efficacy in HCPS and PUUV-caused HFRS is attributed to the rapid clinical progression of these diseases, which often leaves a narrow window for intervention before the onset of irreversible organ failure (Heyman et al., 2009; Vaheri et al., 2013a; Strella et al., 2025). Originally discovered by Toyama Chemical Co., Ltd., during a screening for anti-influenza compounds, the prodrug favipiravir (T- 705) has emerged as a potent viral replication inhibitor. Upon cellular entry, host enzymes convert favipiravir into its active form, favipiravir-RTP. This active metabolite functions as a purine nucleotide analogue that is incorporated into nascent viral RNA, inducing lethal mutagenesis in the viral genome (Furuta et al., 2009, 2017). Safronetz et al. (2013) have shown that favipiravir potently inhibited ANDV and SNV in vitro, and provided 100% survival in lethal ANDV hamster models when treatment was initiated before viremia, making it an important drug candidate for post-exposure prophylaxis. To further enhance clinical outcomes, Mayor et al. (2021) combined the use of favipiravir with ribavirin to achieve synergistic orthohantavirus inhibition. papers.title: Hantavirus emergence through a One Health lens: ecological dynamics, human exposure and integrated surveillance
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic viruses that cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas. Although human hantavirus infections are usually recognised clinically, infection risk is affected by upstream factors including reservoir-host ecology, environmental variability and human exposure. Evidence from China, Europe and the Americas shows that the incidence of hantavirus may depend on rodent population dynamics, climate conditions, land use, agricultural practices, housing environments and recreational or travel-related exposure. In China, the seasonal pattern of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, including a major autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak in many endemic areas, illustrates how virus–host ecology and agricultural labour jointly affect the human risk. In Europe, bank vole population cycles have been shown to influence Puumala virus epidemics, while studies in the Americas have linked rainfall, rodent abundance and human exposure in domestic, occupational and recreational settings. This mini review synthesises evidence on the ecological drivers, exposure pathways and surveillance challenges for hantavirus diseases through a One Health lens. We suggest that One Health approaches should move beyond general calls for multisector collaboration towards evidence-informed surveillance linking rodent, environmental and human data to setting-specific prevention, such as issuing seasonal risk warnings and reinforcing exposure-reduction measures before harvest periods in endemic agricultural regions.
