Hantavirus emergence through a One Health lens: ecological dynamics, human exposure and integrated surveillance Xinyu Wang1,2* Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic viruses that cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas. Although human hantavirus infections are usually recognised clinically, infection risk is affected by upstream factors including reservoir-host ecology, environmental variability and human exposure. Evidence from China, Europe and the Americas shows that the incidence of hantavi- rus may depend on rodent population dynamics, climate conditions, land use, agricultural practices, housing environ- ments and recreational or travel-related exposure. In China, the seasonal pattern of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, including a major autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak in many endemic areas, illustrates how virus–host ecology and agricultural labour jointly affect the human risk. In Europe, bank vole population cycles have been shown to influence Puumala virus epidemics, while studies in the Americas have linked rainfall, rodent abundance and human exposure in domestic, occupational and recreational settings. This mini review synthesises evidence on the ecological drivers, exposure pathways and surveillance challenges for hantavirus diseases through a One Health lens. We suggest that One Health approaches should move beyond general calls for multisec- tor collaboration towards evidence-informed surveillance linking rodent, environmental and human data to setting- specific prevention, such as issuing seasonal risk warnings and reinforcing exposure-reduction measures before har- vest periods in endemic agricultural regions. Keywords Hantavirus, One Health, Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, Rodent reservoir, Ecological surveillance, China, Travel medicine Introduction The epidemiology of hantaviruses is tightly linked to res- ervoir hosts, environmental conditions and human expo- sure, making them a useful model for reviewing zoonotic emergence through a One Health lens. Medically impor- tant hantaviruses are maintained primarily in rodent reservoirs and are associated with two major human disease syndromes: haemorrhagic fever with renal syn- drome (HFRS), reported mainly in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS; also his- torically referred to as hantavirus pulmonary syndrome), reported mainly in the Americas [1–3]. Human infec- tion is usually accidental and occurs when people enter environments contaminated by infectious rodent excreta; however, Andes virus remains the major exception, with documented person-to-person transmission under con- ditions of close or prolonged contact [3, 4]. Rather than cataloguing hantavirus species, this review focuses on synthesising the evidence for how ecological *Correspondence: Xinyu Wang snowmed@gmail.com 1 Department of Infectious Diseases, Huashan Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai 200040, China 2 National Medical Center for Infectious Diseases, Shanghai 200040, China Page 2 of 7 Wang ﻿One Health Advances (2026) 4:36 and social processes shape human infection. Key ques- tions are not only which virus is carried by which rodent, but under what environmental and behavioural condi- tions infected reservoirs and susceptible humans are brought into contact. This framing is relevant for the One Health approach, because hantavirus risk can be exam- ined across measurable links including the rodent popu- lation density, reservoir-infection prevalence, climate variability, land use, agricultural or occupational expo- sure, housing conditions, recreational travel and clinical surveillance [1, 5]. China’s long-standing HFRS experi- ence, Europe’s cyclic Puumala virus epidemics and HCPS outbreaks in the Americas collectively provide comple- mentary evidence for understanding hantavirus emer- gence as an integrated human–animal–environment problem. This makes hantavirus disease a useful case for examining how the One Health approach can move from a conceptual framework to measurable surveillance indi- cators and setting-specific prevention. Reservoir ecology and environmental drivers of hantavirus risk The geographic distribution of hantavirus infection is strongly affected by its reservoir-host ecology. Although an increasing variety of hantaviruses have been detected in mammals, medically important hantaviruses are mainly maintained in rodent reservoirs, and many patho- genic viruses show close associations with particular host species or host complexes [1, 2]. This host dependence helps to explain the geographically uneven hantavirus risk, with human disease only occurring where compe- tent reservoirs, suitable habitats and human exposure all overlap. However, reservoir presence alone is insuf- ficient to predict human risk, and the local incidence also depends on rodent abundance, infection prevalence within reservoir populations, seasonal movement, habi- tat disturbance and the frequency with which humans enter contaminated environments [5]. Environmental variability can influence hantavirus transmission by changing the reservoir-host population dynamics and human–rodent contact. Increased rain- fall may enhance vegetation growth and food availabil- ity for rodents, thus supporting their reproduction and survival, while drought, habitat disruption or cold stress may drive rodents into human dwellings, storage areas or workplaces. The Four Corners region of the southwestern United States remains a classic example, where El Niño- associated precipitation led to ecological conditions that favoured increases in deer mouse populations, with a subsequent marked increase in HCPS cases in affected areas [6]. In Europe, Puumala virus epidemics have been linked to bank vole population cycles influenced by for- est ecology, food availability and seasonal conditions [7]. These examples suggest that climate is not a direct cause in isolation, but can influence risk via reservoir ecology and exposure pathways. Because human hantavirus cases often occur after changes in reservoir populations, rodent abundance and infection prevalence can act as early-warning indicators. Long-term ecological studies in Europe and the Americas have shown that rodent population cycles may precede changes in human disease risk [6, 7]. In China, ecologi- cal studies of HFRS have also emphasised the interacting roles of environmental variability, reservoir ecology and human behaviour in shaping disease dynamics [5]. These findings support a practical One Health implication: rodent monitoring should not be treated solely as ecolog- ical research, but as part of an integrated risk-assessment system linking animal, environmental and human health data. Land use, agriculture and human exposure: evidence from China and beyond Land use determines how often reservoir hosts, con- taminated environments and susceptible humans share the same space. Agricultural expansion, crop harvesting, grain storage, peri-domestic farming structures, forest edges and poorly sealed rural housing can increase the opportunities for contact with rodent excreta. A system- atic review of land cover, land use and human hantavi- rus infection risk found that agricultural land use was positively associated with infection risk in several set- tings, particularly in China and Brazil, whereas associa- tions with forest cover, grassland or built-up areas varied by region and virus ecology [8]. This heterogeneity is important, in that land use is not a universal risk factor but rather modifies exposure through local combinations of reservoir species, farming systems, housing conditions and human behaviour. China provides one of the clearest examples of how virus ecology and human activity jointly structure hanta- virus seasonality. In many endemic areas, HFRS shows a bimodal pattern, with a larger autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak. In China, this bimodal pattern has often been interpreted as reflect- ing the coexistence of different virus–host systems and exposure settings. Hantaan virus, mainly associated with Apodemus agrarius, contributes more to field or rural exposure and autumn–winter incidence, whereas Seoul virus, carried by Rattus norvegicus, is more relevant to peri-domestic or urban transmission and spring inci- dence in many settings [9–11]. In Zibo City, HFRS cases peaked during March–May and October–December, illustrating the seasonal human risk pattern [9]. Spatial analyses from the same region further suggested that Page 3 of 7 Wang ﻿One Health Advances (2026) 4:36 spring and autumn risks differed geographically, support- ing targeted seasonal prevention [12]. The link between agricultural activity and HFRS sea- sonality is particularly evident in high-incidence prov- inces such as Shandong. A time-series analysis reported marked seasonality and discussed the temporal cor- respondence between agricultural activity and HFRS incidence: the autumn harvest usually begins in late September, cases then rise rapidly in October, peak in November, and decline in December [13]. The incubation period of hantavirus infection suggests that this pattern is biologically plausible and consistent with exposure dur- ing harvesting, field work, grain handling or temporary accommodation in rodent-infested settings. Together with the smaller spring peak observed in many endemic areas, this pattern suggests that HFRS risk is shaped by seasonally changing combinations of reservoir ecology, agricultural labour and peri-domestic exposure, rather than by a single constant pathway. In addition to agriculture, hantavirus exposure may occur in occupational, domestic, recreational and travel settings. Farmers, forestry workers, construction work- ers, cleaners, military personnel and people entering rodent-infested buildings may experience intense short- term exposure when contaminated dust is disturbed. Recreational exposure can occur when visitors stay in cabins, campsites or enclosed structures with rodent infestation. The 2012 Yosemite National Park outbreak, linked to overnight stays in insulated tent cabins, showed how built environments can convert local rodent ecology into visitor risk [14]. The 2026 cruise-associated Andes virus cluster illustrates a different pathway, with local ecological exposure potentially becoming a multi-coun- try public health problem when combined with delayed recognition, confined travel settings and international movements [15]. Surveillance evidence and gaps across human– animal–environment systems China’s long-term HFRS experience provides an instruc- tive example of surveillance that already contains several One Health elements, even if not always labelled as such. National surveillance has combined human case report- ing with rodent surveillance, laboratory testing and tar- geted prevention in endemic areas. During 2006–2012, 77,558 HFRS cases and 866 deaths were reported in China. Cases were clustered in a small number of prov- inces and occurring mainly in spring and autumn–win- ter seasons, with farmers remaining the largest affected occupational group [10]. More recent national data for 2014–2023 show continuing geographic and virological complexity, with Hantaan virus, Seoul virus and Puu- mala virus among the identified human HFRS-associated hantaviruses in China [11]. These regional contrasts are summarised in Table 1, which compares rodent, envi- ronmental and human surveillance components across China, Europe and the Americas. Despite the value of long-term case reporting, human surveillance alone is inherently too late for hantavirus prevention, and human cases usually only appear after ecological changes, rodent population shifts and expo- sure events have already occurred. Clinical recogni- tion may also be delayed because the early symptoms are non-specific and overlap with leptospirosis, dengue, influenza-like illness, malaria, COVID-19 and other febrile syndromes [3]. This is particularly relevant in rural or travel-related settings, where the exposure event may be remote in time and place from the diagnosis. For surveillance to support prevention rather than only documentation, clinical signals should be connected with rodent, environmental and exposure information. In clinical practice, a compatible syndrome combined with a carefully reconstructed exposure history—such as recent rural residence, crop harvesting, cleaning of rodent-infested spaces, cabin stay or expedition travel— may provide the first actionable signal before laboratory confirmation. The One Health challenge is therefore not simply to collect more data, but to link the appropriate data to timely decisions. Information on rodent density, reser- voir infection prevalence, climate anomalies, agricultural calendars, land-use changes, clinical syndromes and travel or occupational histories is often held by different sectors and interpreted separately. Broader One Health early-warning literature emphasises the importance of bottom-up reporting and grassroots actors for reduc- ing delays between outbreak emergence, notification and response [16]. For hantavirus diseases, integrated early warning should therefore be judged not by the number of assembled datasets, but by whether ecological and clinical signals lead to earlier, setting-specific preven- tion. Future surveillance should therefore be built around predefined risk questions and response thresholds rather than around parallel human, animal and environmental datasets. In resource-limited settings, integrated One Health surveillance should not aim to monitor every possible ecological, animal and human indicator. A more feasible approach is to develop a minimum surveillance package tailored to local risk settings, combining routine report- ing of compatible human syndromes, simple rodent-den- sity indicators, seasonal agricultural calendars, rainfall or flooding alerts, community reports of rodent infestation and exposure histories collected during clinical assess- ment. Hantavirus emergence through a One Health lens: ecological dynamics, human exposure and integrated surveillance Xinyu Wang1,2* Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic viruses that cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas. Although human hantavirus infections are usually recognised clinically, infection risk is affected by upstream factors including reservoir-host ecology, environmental variability and human exposure. Evidence from China, Europe and the Americas shows that the incidence of hantavi- rus may depend on rodent population dynamics, climate conditions, land use, agricultural practices, housing environ- ments and recreational or travel-related exposure. In China, the seasonal pattern of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, including a major autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak in many endemic areas, illustrates how virus–host ecology and agricultural labour jointly affect the human risk. In Europe, bank vole population cycles have been shown to influence Puumala virus epidemics, while studies in the Americas have linked rainfall, rodent abundance and human exposure in domestic, occupational and recreational settings. This mini review synthesises evidence on the ecological drivers, exposure pathways and surveillance challenges for hantavirus diseases through a One Health lens. We suggest that One Health approaches should move beyond general calls for multisec- tor collaboration towards evidence-informed surveillance linking rodent, environmental and human data to setting- specific prevention, such as issuing seasonal risk warnings and reinforcing exposure-reduction measures before har- vest periods in endemic agricultural regions. Keywords Hantavirus, One Health, Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, Rodent reservoir, Ecological surveillance, China, Travel medicine Introduction The epidemiology of hantaviruses is tightly linked to res- ervoir hosts, environmental conditions and human expo- sure, making them a useful model for reviewing zoonotic emergence through a One Health lens. Medically impor- tant hantaviruses are maintained primarily in rodent reservoirs and are associated with two major human disease syndromes: haemorrhagic fever with renal syn- drome (HFRS), reported mainly in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS; also his- torically referred to as hantavirus pulmonary syndrome), reported mainly in the Americas [1–3]. Human infec- tion is usually accidental and occurs when people enter environments contaminated by infectious rodent excreta; however, Andes virus remains the major exception, with documented person-to-person transmission under con- ditions of close or prolonged contact [3, 4]. Rather than cataloguing hantavirus species, this review focuses on synthesising the evidence for how ecological *Correspondence: Xinyu Wang snowmed@gmail.com 1 Department of Infectious Diseases, Huashan Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai 200040, China 2 National Medical Center for Infectious Diseases, Shanghai 200040, China Page 2 of 7 Wang ﻿One Health Advances (2026) 4:36 and social processes shape human infection. Key ques- tions are not only which virus is carried by which rodent, but under what environmental and behavioural condi- tions infected reservoirs and susceptible humans are brought into contact. This framing is relevant for the One Health approach, because hantavirus risk can be exam- ined across measurable links including the rodent popu- lation density, reservoir-infection prevalence, climate variability, land use, agricultural or occupational expo- sure, housing conditions, recreational travel and clinical surveillance [1, 5]. China’s long-standing HFRS experi- ence, Europe’s cyclic Puumala virus epidemics and HCPS outbreaks in the Americas collectively provide comple- mentary evidence for understanding hantavirus emer- gence as an integrated human–animal–environment problem. This makes hantavirus disease a useful case for examining how the One Health approach can move from a conceptual framework to measurable surveillance indi- cators and setting-specific prevention. Reservoir ecology and environmental drivers of hantavirus risk The geographic distribution of hantavirus infection is strongly affected by its reservoir-host ecology. Although an increasing variety of hantaviruses have been detected in mammals, medically important hantaviruses are mainly maintained in rodent reservoirs, and many patho- genic viruses show close associations with particular host species or host complexes [1, 2]. This host dependence helps to explain the geographically uneven hantavirus risk, with human disease only occurring where compe- tent reservoirs, suitable habitats and human exposure all overlap. However, reservoir presence alone is insuf- ficient to predict human risk, and the local incidence also depends on rodent abundance, infection prevalence within reservoir populations, seasonal movement, habi- tat disturbance and the frequency with which humans enter contaminated environments [5]. Environmental variability can influence hantavirus transmission by changing the reservoir-host population dynamics and human–rodent contact. Increased rain- fall may enhance vegetation growth and food availabil- ity for rodents, thus supporting their reproduction and survival, while drought, habitat disruption or cold stress may drive rodents into human dwellings, storage areas or workplaces. The Four Corners region of the southwestern United States remains a classic example, where El Niño- associated precipitation led to ecological conditions that favoured increases in deer mouse populations, with a subsequent marked increase in HCPS cases in affected areas [6]. In Europe, Puumala virus epidemics have been linked to bank vole population cycles influenced by for- est ecology, food availability and seasonal conditions [7]. These examples suggest that climate is not a direct cause in isolation, but can influence risk via reservoir ecology and exposure pathways. Because human hantavirus cases often occur after changes in reservoir populations, rodent abundance and infection prevalence can act as early-warning indicators. Long-term ecological studies in Europe and the Americas have shown that rodent population cycles may precede changes in human disease risk [6, 7]. In China, ecologi- cal studies of HFRS have also emphasised the interacting roles of environmental variability, reservoir ecology and human behaviour in shaping disease dynamics [5]. These findings support a practical One Health implication: rodent monitoring should not be treated solely as ecolog- ical research, but as part of an integrated risk-assessment system linking animal, environmental and human health data. analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒es 是啮齿动物传播的动物源性病毒,可导致欧亚地区的肾综合征出血热和美洲的 汉坦病毒心肺综合征,其风险受储宿主生态、环境变异性和人类暴露的影响。
analysis_zh.methods: 本小型综述综合了关于生态驱动因素、暴露途径以及在中国、欧洲和美洲的 汉坦病毒 疾病监测挑战的证据。
analysis_zh.results: 证据表明发病率可能取决于啮齿动物种群动态、气候、土地利用、农业实践、居住和娱乐暴露;中国出现肾综合征出血热的秋冬季和春季高峰,欧洲的田鼠循环影响 普马拉病毒 流行,美洲的研究将降雨、啮齿动物丰度以及职业/娱乐暴露与病例关联。
analysis_zh.contribution: 作者建议 One Health 方法应超越笼统的多部门呼吁,转向基于证据的监测,将啮齿动物、环境和人类数据关联,实现针对特定情境的防控,如季节性风险预警和收获前的暴露降低措施。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告局限性。

papers.title: Human Orthohantavirus infections: From virology and clinical epidemiology to oral biological features and dental practice
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic pathogens responsible for 2 severe clinical syndromes in humans: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), affecting an estimated 150,000 to 200,000 individuals annually worldwide, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), characterized by fulminant pulmonary edema with case fatality rates approaching 40%. Although the systemic manifestations of hantavirus disease are well described, the oral and salivary dimensions of infection have received comparatively little attention in the dental literature. This review synthesizes current evidence on the virology, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, oral complications, diagnostic approaches, treatment options, and dental practice implications of human hantavirus infections. A narrative review with a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar was conducted, supplemented by hand-searching and by consultation of the World Health Organization and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control outbreak reporting. Particular attention was directed toward primary research on salivary immunity, oral fluid diagnostics, and salivary gland tropism. Andes virus (ANDV) antigen has been detected in secretory cells of human salivary glands, and ANDV uniquely resists the antiviral capacity of human saliva, providing a biologically plausible mechanism for its person-to-person transmissibility. Infectious virus has since been recovered from saliva and gingival crevicular fluid during acute infection, although a salivary route of transmission remains an epidemiological association rather than proven. In a cohort of 69 confirmed ANDV-infected cases, salivary secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) was significantly elevated (4.846 vs. 0.333 mg/mL in exposed-uninfected contacts), whereas mucins MUC7 and MUC5B were more frequently detected in exposed-but-not-infected household contacts, a cross-sectional finding whose direction of causation is unresolved. Total salivary sIgA is a non-specific marker of mucosal immune activation and has no pathogen specificity. Oral fluid IgM assays for Hantaan virus achieved 96.7% sensitivity and 94.9% specificity against serum reference, supporting further evaluation of non-invasive salivary surveillance. Clinically, severe sore throat persisting for 2 to 3 weeks and oropharyngeal edema are documented as early features of hantavirus infection. Thrombocytopenia, which may be profound during the oliguric phase of HFRS, confers significant oral hemorrhagic risk. Human hantavirus infection presents with clinically significant oral and salivary manifestations that are directly relevant to dental practitioners. Dental teams should be aware of the hemorrhagic risk in patients with thrombocytopenia, the aerosol risk in patients with HCPS, the theoretical risk of ANDV transmission via oral contact in endemic regions, and the emerging utility of salivary diagnostics. Recommendations for dental practice are extrapolated from medical, virological, and general infection control evidence, rather than from dental clinical research, and are identified as precautionary where that is the case.

papers.title: Multi-host circulation and evolutionary dynamics of hantaviruses in small mammals in Southwestern China
papers.abstract: China represents a major hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS)-endemic region, where small mammals, particularly rodents, constitute the principal reservoir hosts. This study characterized HV diversity, RNA detection rate, host range, evolutionary history, and tissue distribution in 1 717 wild small mammals collected from Yunnan Province, China. HVs were detected in 47 animals, corresponding to an overall RNA detection rate of 2.74% (47/1 717, 95% CI: 1.97%–3.51%). At least five HV species or lineages were identified across 10 small mammal species, including Orthohantavirus luxiense (LUXV), Orthohantavirus fugongense (FUGV), Orthohantavirus seoulense (SEOV), Orthohantavirus caobangense (CBNV), and Thottimvirus sp. Host‐virus coevolutionary analysis suggested extensive interspecies transmission, with particularly strong support for phylogenetically inferred host‐switching events involving SEOV and FUGV. Preliminary analysis of tissue viral loads revealed that LUXV was widely distributed across various tissues and that significant differences in viral levels existed among tissues (χ2 = 27.500, P < 0.001). Collectively, these findings elucidate the genetic diversity and evolutionary dynamics of HVs in small mammals in Yunnan.

analysis_zh.results: 在47只动物中检测到汉坦病毒RNA(总体检出率为2.74%,95%置信区间1.97%–3.51%)。在10种小型哺乳动物中鉴定出至少五种汉坦病毒种/系(LUXV、FUGV、SEOV、CBNV、Thottimvirus sp.)。共进化分析提示存在广泛的跨种传播,并对涉及SEOV和FUGV的宿主转换事件提供了强有力的支持。组织分析显示LUXV在各器官中广泛分布,组织间病毒载量差异显著(χ2 = 27.500,P < 0.001)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些发现阐明了汉坦病毒在云南小型哺乳动物中的遗传多样性和进化动态,为监测和公共卫生风险评估提供了宝贵信息。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告任何局限性。

papers.title: Vaccines Against Hantavirus Infections: A Systematic Literature Review
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hantaviruses infections are responsible for a hemorrhagic fever with renal and cardiopulmonary syndrome with case-fatality rates up to 50%. While inactivated vaccines are already available in China and South Korea, several additional candidate vaccines are under development. This systematic review summarizes the current clinical evidence on immunogenicity and short-term safety of vaccines targeting different hantavirus strains. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic literature search was carried out to identify randomized and nonrandomized trials of any phase. Data were synthesized narratively within strata defined by vaccine platform, target virus, assay, immunogenicity and safety. Results: Ten trials on 961 adults were included: four single-arm trials on the inactivated vaccine and six early-phase DNA-vaccine trials. One month after last dose, the inactivated vaccine achieved neutralizing seropositivity by PRNT50 in 45.1% of the tested subjects after two priming doses and 55.7% after three, while the corresponding binding-antibody values measured by IFA were 87.3% and 95.7%. Among DNA vaccines, homologous responses reached 100% against HTNV and 83.3% against PUUV with monovalent constructs, whereas dual responses to the bivalent construct were registered in 33.3% and 77.8% of the subjects, when measured through PRNT50 and PsVNA50, respectively. One serious adverse event occurred, most likely unrelated to vaccination. Conclusions: No serious safety signal was identified, although safety remains insufficiently characterized. Measured immunogenicity depends as much on the assay as on the vaccine, and, in the absence of a validated correlate of protection, it cannot be read as a clinical benefit. Future research should prioritize validated correlates of protection and innovative trial designs adapted to low-incidence diseases.

papers.title_zh: 针对 汉坦病毒 感染的疫苗:系统文献综述

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 感染导致严重的肾综合征出血热和汉坦病毒心肺综合征,病例致死率最高可达50% (A1)。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述聚焦于疫苗平台——目前在中国和韩国使用的灭活疫苗以及早期阶段的DNA疫苗——以及它们的免疫原性和安全性概况 (A2, A6, A7, A8)。

analysis_zh.future_research: 未来研究应建立经验证的保护相关指标,并采用适用于低发病率 汉坦病毒 疾病的创新试验设计 (A12)。

papers.title: Transmission timing and containment risk in human Andes virus outbreaks
papers.abstract: Abstract The 2026 multinational Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak linked to cruise-ship travel from Argentina triggered extensive contact tracing and quarantine. Whether intervention on this scale was necessary or sufficient depends on the risk of onward transmission, which can be difficult to estimate early in an outbreak. Using transmission-pair data from the 2018–2019 outbreak in Epuyén, Argentina, and a mechanistic model linking viral growth, symptom onset, and transmission, we estimated that 42.4% (95% CrI: 18.2–69.7%) of transmission occurs before symptom onset and that the median incubation period is 18.5 days (95% CrI: 16.5–19.5). We simulated outbreaks under an Epuyén-calibrated estimate (R = 2.12, k = 0.316) and a pooled estimate from 15 prior ANDV investigations (R = 0.24, k = 0.39), with intervention beginning after two generations, as in the cruise-associated event. Under the higher-transmission scenario, missing 10% of exposed individuals or downstream contacts resulted in a 29.9% probability of continued spread and a 20.6% probability that at least 5,000 ultimately uninfected people would be quarantined. Under lower transmission, continued spread stayed below 8%. However, the risk of onward transmission could not be estimated precisely from the first several detected cases. Whether intervention on this scale was necessary or sufficient depends on the risk of onward transmission, which can be difficult to estimate early in an outbreak. Using transmission-pair data from the 2018–2019 outbreak in Epuyén, Argentina, and a mechanistic model linking viral growth, symptom onset, and transmission, we estimated that 42.4% (95% CrI: 18.2–69.7%) of transmission occurs before symptom onset and that the median incubation period is 18.5 days (95% CrI: 16.5–19.5). We simulated outbreaks under an Epuyén-calibrated estimate (R = 2.12, k = 0.316) and a pooled estimate from 15 prior ANDV investigations (R = 0.24, k = 0.39), with intervention beginning after two generations, as in the cruise-associated event. Under the higher-transmission scenario, missing 10% of exposed individuals or downstream contacts resulted in a 29.9% probability of continued spread and a 20.6% probability that at least 5,000 ultimately uninfected people would be quarantined. Under lower transmission, continued spread stayed below 8%. However, the risk of onward transmission could not be estimated precisely from the first several detected cases. These findings therefore support rapid, comprehensive contact tracing and quarantine after large international exposure events despite substantial costs. 1 Introduction Andes virus (ANDV) is the only hantavirus known to be capable of person-to-person transmission, although documented transmission has been confined to a small number of localized outbreaks [1– 3]. ANDV infection is associated with a case-fatality rate of approximately 36% [4], and there are currently no approved vaccines or specific antiviral therapies. Recent increases in ANDV activity in South America have heightened concern about the potential for person-to-person spread [5]. In 2026, a multinational ANDV exposure event linked to cruise-ship travel from Argentina led to 13 reported cases and 3 deaths, and prompted extensive international contact tracing and prolonged quarantine of 147 passengers and crew from 23 countries [6, 7]. The severity of ANDV disease and its potential for person-to-person spread may warrant such intensive responses, but evidence on their effectiveness and associated quarantine burden remains limited. Evaluating containment strategies requires a detailed understanding of ANDV transmission dy- namics. Decisions about the scale and duration of contact tracing and quarantine depend on incu- bation periods, the timing of infectiousness relative to symptom onset, and individual-level variation in transmission. Long incubation periods prolong monitoring and quarantine, transmission before symptom onset allows infected individuals to spread infection before they are recognized and iso- lated, and variation in transmission means that a small number of infected individuals may account for a disproportionate share of secondary infections. However, estimating these quantities from outbreak data is complicated by evolving control measures, including case detection, isolation, and quarantine, which alter transmission opportunities over time. The 2018–2019 Epuyén outbreak provides the most detailed empirical data on person-to-person ANDV transmission. The original outbreak investigation reconstructed transmission chains, identi- fied superspreading, and estimated that the effective reproduction number (Re) declined from 2.12 before implementation of isolation and quarantine to 0.96 afterward [13]. Most reported ANDV infections, by contrast, arise from zoonotic spillover and are not followed by sustained person-to- person transmission. Transmission in Epuyén concentrated at a birthday party and a wake, in a town of fewer than 2,000 people, suggesting that what distinguishes these outcomes is not where infection is acquired but the number and intensity of close contacts during the brief window around symptom onset, variation in infectiousness across individuals, or both. The relative contributions of contact and infectiousness cannot be resolved from existing investigations, which report secondary cases but not contacts that did not result in transmission. Because incubation can last several weeks, the setting an infected person occupies during the transmission window may differ substan- tially from the setting in which exposure occurred. Transmission potential can therefore vary among cases, locations, and generations of the same outbreak. More recently, a latent-time analysis of the Epuyén transmission-pair data jointly estimated unobserved infection times, generation intervals, transmission timing relative to source symptom onset, time-varying reproduction numbers, and offspring dispersion from interval-censored data [12]. However, it modeled incubation and transmission timing as separate empirical delay distributions rather than as outcomes of a shared within-host process. This limited its ability to represent 2 biological dependencies among infection, symptom onset, and infectiousness. Here, we extend the latent-time framework by integrating a mechanistic model that jointly links infection, symptom onset, and transmission [15]. We incorporate the resulting estimates in stochastic branching-process simulations of a multinational exposure event based on the initial timing and magnitude of the 2026 cruise-associated outbreak. Given the variation in transmission observed across past ANDV events, we simulate outbreaks in both high- and low-transmission settings. The high-transmission setting uses parameters estimated from the Epuyén investigation, whereas the low-transmission setting uses pooled estimates from 15 prior ANDV investigations. We estimate the level of contact tracing and quarantine required for containment and quantify the consequences of incomplete or delayed intervention. Results We fitted the within-host-informed latent-time model to 34 cases and 33 reconstructed source- recipient pairs from the 2018–2019 Epuyén outbreak in Argentina (Table 1; Figure 1). Transmission was concentrated near source symptom onset, with an estimated 42.4% of transmission events oc- curring before symptoms appeared (95% CrI: 18.2–69.7%). The median transmission time was 0.07 days after source symptom onset (95% CrI: (-0.20) to 0.30 days), and the central 95% of transmission events occurred from 0.85 days before to 2.02 days after source symptom onset (Figure 1A). The median incubation period was 18.50 days (95% CrI: 16.50–19.50 days), with a central 95% distributional interval of 7.50–35.50 days (Figure 1C). An estimated 95% of infections developed symptoms by 31.50 days (95% CrI: 29.50–35.50), and 99% by 39.50 days (95% CrI: 35.50–44.50). The median generation interval was 22.50 days (95% CrI: 20.50–23.50 days) (Figure 1B), and the median serial interval was 21.79 days (95% CrI: 21.28–22.18 days) (Figure 1D). Thus, exposed individuals may require several weeks of follow-up even though onward transmission is concentrated within a narrow window around symptom onset. These estimates were broadly consistent with previous analyses of the Epuyén outbreak while providing model-based inference of latent infection times and transmission timing relative to symptom onset (Supplementary Results). Table 1: Estimated epidemiological characteristics of person-to-person ANDV trans- mission. Median estimates are reported with 95% credible intervals (CrIs), reflecting uncertainty in the estimated population median. The central 95% interval summarizes the expected range across individual infections or transmission events. Transmission timing is reported relative to source symptom onset, with negative values indicating transmission before symptom onset. Quantity Median estimate (95% CrI) Central 95% interval Incubation period 18.50 days (16.50–19.50) 7.50–35.50 days Latent period 13.50 days (10.50–15.50) 5.50–22.50 days Generation interval 22.50 days (20.50–23.50) 12.50–38.50 days Serial interval 21.79 days (21.28–22.18) 12.20–36.94 days Transmission timing (relative to symptom onset) 0.07 days (−0.20–0.30) −0.85–2.02 days 3 Figure 1: Estimated epidemiological timing distributions for person-to-person ANDV transmission. Panels show the inferred distributions of the (A) transmission timing relative to source symptom onset, (B) generation interval, (C) incubation period, and (D) serial interval. Solid curves represent posterior median densities, and shaded regions indicate the corresponding 95% credible intervals. Dashed vertical lines mark zero days. In panel A, negative values indicate transmission before source symptom onset; in panel D, negative values indicate that the recipient developed symptoms before the source case. To characterize the transmission conditions documented across settings, we analyzed 15 pub- lished ANDV investigations. A hierarchical negative-binomial model estimated a pooled reproduc- tion number of 0.24 (95% CrI: 0.12–0.48) and a shared dispersion parameter of 0.39 (95% CrI: 0.19–0.89), reflecting low average but highly variable realized transmission across this broader set of investigations. Together with the Epuyén-calibrated estimates (R=2.12, k=0.316), these results anchored an empirically informed range of ANDV transmission potential. Hereafter, we refer to simulations using the Epuyén and pooled parameterizations as the higher- and lower-transmission scenarios, respectively. The primary analysis reproduced the timing of the 2026 cruise-associated response, with inter- vention beginning on simulation day 35, 26 days after symptom onset in the first detected case. 4 We restricted the analysis to outbreaks that had reached at least two generations of transmission by then; this occurred in approximately 35% of higher-transmission simulations and 3% of lower- transmission simulations. Tracing failures had substantially greater consequences under higher transmission (Figure 2A). When tracing missed 5%, 10%, 25%, or 50% of exposed individuals or downstream contacts, post-response transmission outside quarantine occurred in 18.9%, 29.9%, 51.1%, and 70.8% of simulations, respectively. Under the lower transmission, this probability ranged from 0.7% with 5% missed to 7.8% with 50% missed. Among simulations with higher transmission and at least one additional post-response infection, missing 10% of contacts resulted in a median of 5 additional infections and a 95th percentile of 49. With 25% or 50% missed, the medians increased to 8 and 27, respectively, and the 95th percentiles to 111 and 351. With lower transmission, the median remained between one and two across tracing levels (Figure 2B). Quarantine burdens were substantially lower under lower transmission (Figure 2C). With 10% of contacts missed, the median number of retrospectively uninfected downstream contacts quaran- tined was 313 (IQR 185–440), compared with 1,821 (IQR 720–4,161) under the higher-transmission scenario. At lower transmission, the median burden fell by 49%, from 329 with complete tracing to 167 with 50% of contacts missed, because outbreaks were small and fewer contacts were traced. At higher transmission, fewer quarantines per case were offset by larger outbreaks and more tracing events, leaving the median comparatively stable but increasing the risk of very large quarantine burdens. Most response activity ended within the initial six-week quarantine period, but breakthrough transmission occasionally prolonged the response under the higher-transmission scenario. With 10% of contacts missed, the median additional response duration was zero months, the 95th percentile was 1.61 months, and 0.2% of simulations required at least four additional months of response activity. With 50% missed, the median increased to 1.02 months and the 95th percentile to 5.01 months. With lower transmission, additional response duration remained near zero (Figure 2D). The multinational response to the 2026 cruise-associated outbreak was initiated after seven confirmed or suspected cases were identified. To assess the consequences of delayed intervention, we initiated contact tracing and quarantine after different numbers of cases had been reported, assuming 95% tracing completeness (Figure 3). Under higher transmission, delaying intervention from the first to the twentieth reported case increased the probability of at least 100 infections from 2.7% to 38.2% and of at least 500 infections from 2.1% to 14.0%. Median outbreak size increased from 1 to 72 infections, median quarantine burden from 2 to 500 individuals, and the probability of quarantining at least 1,000 individuals from 2.7% to 36.0%. Under lower transmission, outbreaks rarely reached the later intervention points: only 13 of 10,000 simulations reached 10 reported cases, and none reached 20. Outcomes following greater delays therefore could not be estimated precisely. Under active containment, most simulated outbreaks ended before enough cases were detected to estimate the reproduction number precisely. Estimates from the first few detected cases were highly uncertain, with broad 95% credible intervals that commonly included R = 1 under both transmission scenarios (Supplementary Figure 5). (D) Additional response duration beyond the initial six-week quarantine period; outcomes were summarized across all conditioned simulations, with points showing medians and upper error bars showing the 95th percentile. However, the size of the 2026 cruise-associated outbreak was much more probable under higher transmission: outbreaks of at least 13 cases occurred in 29.4% of higher-transmission simulations compared with 0.01% of lower- transmission simulations. Beyond final outbreak size, the observed timing of case accumulation was also poorly compatible with the pooled parameterization (pcompat = 0.0055). Nevertheless, this parameterization occasionally produced outbreaks of the observed magnitude. Simulations assumed 95% tracing completeness and varied the number of reported cases after which tracing and quarantine were initiated. Panels show the estimated distributions of (A) total infections and (B) individuals requiring quarantine under the higher-transmission (gray) and lower-transmission (black) scenarios across 10,000 stochastic simula- tions per transmission scenario and intervention delay. For each reported-case trigger, boxplots show the median, interquartile range, and 1.5× interquartile-range whiskers; points represent individual simulations beyond the whiskers. Outcomes were summarized among simulations that reached the specified reported-case trigger. The y-axes are shown on a logarithmic scale to visualize the highly right-skewed outcome distributions. The transmission scenarios were therefore difficult to distinguish from the first few detected cases: within-outbreak 95% credible intervals for R spanned 1 under both scenarios through 5 detected cases (Supplementary Figure 5). Lower-transmission outbreaks rarely reached more than 5 detected cases. This early uncertainty is compounded by the potential for transmission conditions to change as cases disperse into different settings. Methods: It used transmission‑pair data from the 2018–2019 Epuyén outbreak, fitted a mechanistic latent‑time model linking infection, symptom onset, and transmission, and simulated outbreaks under high‑ and low‑transmission scenarios with intervention after two generations. Results: The model estimated 42.4% (95% CrI 18.2–69.7%) of transmission before symptom onset and a median incubation of 18.5 days. papers.title_zh: 人类 安第斯病毒 疫情的传播时机与遏制风险

analysis_zh.background: 本研究针对 安第斯病毒(ANDV)的人人传染风险以及大规模暴露事件后快速遏制的需求,近期暴发使该问题更加突出。
analysis_zh.methods: 研究利用2018–2019年Epuyén暴发的传播配对数据,拟合了将感染、发病和传播关联的机制潜伏期模型,并在高、低传播情景下模拟了在两代传播后介入的疫情。
analysis_zh.results: 模型估计症状出现前的传播占比为42.4%(95%可信区间18.2–69.7%),中位潜伏期为18.5天。在高传播情景下,漏查10%的密切接触导致持续传播的概率为29.9%,且≥5,000人被隔离的概率为20.6%;在低传播情景下,传播率保持在8%以下。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究结果支持在大规模国际暴露事件后迅速、全面开展接触者追踪和隔离,尽管隔离负担沉重。
analysis_zh.limitations: 无法从首例检测病例精确估计后续传播风险,且分析仅限于单一暴发的数据和一篇预印本摘要。

papers.title: Hantavirus species detection from viral genome sequences using explainable artificial intelligence techniques
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are important zoonotic pathogens associated with severe human diseases, including hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recognized the importance of strengthening hantavirus surveillance and early detection because of their public health impact. Nevertheless, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based approaches for hantavirus species identification from viral genome sequences remain largely unexplored. This study developed and evaluated an explainable AI-based approach for hantavirus species identification using viral genome sequence fragments representing six hantavirus species. A transformer-based genomic representation approach (DNABERT-2) was used to generate representations for various Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) models. Sequence redundancy was quantified before model development, and performance was assessed using a 99%-sequence-identity group-aware partitioning strategy with five-fold group-aware cross-validation and an independent internal test set. Direct sequence-similarity auditing confirmed that no sequence pair with ≥ 99% global nucleotide identity crossed the development and test boundary. LightGBM achieved the highest mean group-aware cross-validation performance, with an Accuracy and weighted F1-Score of 99.51%, Cohen’s Kappa coefficient of 99.41%, and Brier Score of 0.19%. On the independent internal test set, LightGBM achieved an Accuracy and weighted F1-Score of 99.25%. SHAP analysis identified influential nucleotide sequence tokens contributing to LightGBM predictions, while a separate DNABERT-2 attention-based analysis identified highly attended nucleotide sequence patterns within the genomic encoder. These findings demonstrate the potential of the proposed approach as an auxiliary method for post-sequencing hantavirus species identification, genomic surveillance, and sequence-based research.

Article in Press Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-75095-x Keywords Hantavirus · Species · Detection · Viral genome sequences · Explainable AI Introduction Hantaviruses are negative-sense, tri-segmented Ribonucleic Acid (RNA) viruses belonging to the family Hanta­ viridae1. They are zoonotic pathogens transmitted primarily to humans through inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected rodent hosts1–3. More than 25 hantavirus species have been associated with human disease4, prin­ cipally causing two major clinical syndromes: Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), predominantly associated with Old World hantaviruses, including Hantaan Orthohantavirus, Orthohantavirus Seoulense, Ortho­ hantavirus Puumalaense, and Orthohantavirus Dobravaense in Europe and Asia; and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS), primarily associated with New World hantaviruses, including Sin Nombre Orthohantavirus and Orthohantavirus Andesense in the Americas4–6. Following an incubation period of approximately 2–4 weeks, both syndromes may initially present with a nonspecific febrile prodromal phase characterized by fever, myalgia, headache, and gastrointestinal symptoms, which can hinder early clinical recognition4,7. Treatment of hantavirus infection is primarily supportive because no widely approved specific antiviral ther­ apy is currently available. Timely recognition of infection may increase clinical awareness of potential complica­ tions and facilitate appropriate monitoring and supportive interventions. Post-mortem case reports have described patients who initially presented to emergency or primary care services with a nonspecific diagnosis of “viral syn­ drome”, without hantavirus infection being considered8–10. Progression to the cardiopulmonary phase of HCPS or the oliguric phase of HFRS is associated with an increased risk of severe complications, mortality, or persistent organ impairment8. Case fatality rates for HCPS can reach 30–50%, while HFRS accounts for tens of thousands of hospitalizations annually across Eurasia4. Disease severity may also differ among hantavirus species, further emphasizing the importance of accurate viral characterization4. Hantaviruses therefore remain important zoonotic pathogens of public health concern because of their potential for emergence, geographic expansion, and association with severe human disease11,12. The World Health Orga­ nization (WHO) has emphasized the importance of strengthening hantavirus surveillance, laboratory capacity, early detection, and outbreak response to reduce the public health impact of these infections13. Recent hantavirus events have further highlighted the need for timely epidemiological investigation, laboratory confirmation, and genomic characterization to support public health decision-making14. Accordingly, accurate characterization of circulating hantavirus species can contribute to genomic surveillance, investigation of viral diversity, and public health preparedness. Laboratory confirmation of hantavirus infection commonly relies on molecular and serological methods, including Reverse Transcription Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) and serological assays, such as Immu­ noglobulin M Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (IgM ELISA)15,16. Following molecular detection, spe­ cies-level characterization can provide additional information for investigating epidemiological patterns, viral diversity, disease-associated differences, and transmission dynamics relevant to public health surveillance17,18. Hantavirus species identification may be performed using species-specific molecular assays or genomic sequence analysis19,20. The increasing availability of viral sequence data therefore provides opportunities for computational approaches that can support post-sequencing species identification. Artificial Intelligence (AI), including Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL), has increasingly been applied in medicine and healthcare data for tasks such as disease detection, diagnosis, and severity predic­ tion21–23. ML methods, such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forest (RF), Decision Tree (DT), and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), can model complex relationships within structured data and have been widely applied across clinical prediction tasks24–26. DL architectures, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), have further expanded the ability to analyze high-dimensional Article in Press Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-75095-x and sequential data21,27,28. More recently, transformer-based models pretrained on genomic sequences have pro­ vided an additional approach for generating contextual representations directly from nucleotide sequence data. Previous applications of AI to hantavirus research have predominantly focused on population-level outbreak or infection-risk prediction rather than species identification from viral nucleotide sequences29–31. For instance, Kazasidis et al. developed an SVM-based early-warning system for predicting annual Orthohantavirus Puuma­ laense outbreaks in Germany, achieving an accuracy of 82.8% using weather variables and beech flowering intensity29. Other computational studies have similarly examined associations among rodent population dynam­ ics, climatic variables, and human hantavirus case counts30,31. Clinical applications have also been investigated. Bulut and Klein developed Kantesti, a multilingual AI-assisted clinical decision-support system that analyzes routine blood-test results to estimate the risk of hantavirus infection32. Following deployment across 50,000 interpreted laboratory reports, the system identified three laboratory-confirmed hantavirus cases that had initially been misclassified by clinicians32. Nevertheless, these approaches address outbreak forecasting, infection-risk assessment, or detection rather than species identification from viral nucleotide sequences29–33. In contrast, AI-based analysis of viral nucleotide sequences has increasingly been investigated for other viruses. Rancati et al. developed DeepAutoCoV, an unsupervised deep autoencoder approach based on SARS- CoV-2 Spike sequences to identify emerging lineages and forecast those likely to become dominant, illustrating the potential of learned sequence representations for genomic surveillance34. Peng et al. developed ViraLM using a pretrained genome foundation model to identify viral sequences directly from nucleotide data, demonstrating the potential of foundation-model representations for viral sequence analysis35. More recently, Rancati et al. introduced SARITA, a generative language model trained on SARS-CoV-2 Spike S1 sequences that generated realistic sequences and reproduced evolutionary patterns associated with subsequently emerging variants36. Anal­ yses across European countries have also demonstrated associations between genomic sequencing activity and epidemiological indicators, further emphasizing the importance of sequence data within pathogen-surveillance frameworks37. Collectively, these studies illustrate the increasing use of AI and language-model-based sequence representations for viral identification, evolutionary analysis, lineage forecasting, and genomic surveillance; nev­ ertheless, corresponding applications to hantavirus species identification remain limited. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, no previous study has investigated AI-based hantavirus species identifi­ cation directly from viral nucleotide sequences while incorporating explainable AI (XAI) techniques for this task. Therefore, this study aimed to develop and evaluate multiple ML and DL models for post-sequencing hantavirus species identification using nucleotide sequence data and representations generated by a pretrained genomic transformer. XAI techniques were additionally incorporated to investigate sequence-level features contribut­ ing to model predictions and to provide complementary exploratory information regarding nucleotide sequence patterns emphasized by the genomic encoder. The proposed approach is intended for post-sequencing genomic analysis, surveillance, and research rather than for the initial diagnosis of hantavirus infection. The findings may contribute to future development of AI-assisted approaches for hantavirus species identification and sequence- based genomic investigation. Materials and methods Figure 1 presents the data-driven AI framework utilized in this study, encompassing dataset preparation, sequence preprocessing and representation generation, model development, performance evaluation, and explainability analysis. Dataset and data preprocessing The dataset comprised 2,571 hantavirus-positive patient-associated records with corresponding viral genome sequence fragments representing six hantavirus species38. The source dataset classified the positive records as Article in Press Scientific Reports https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-75095-x Bayou virus (Orthohantavirus Bayoui), Dobrava virus (Orthohantavirus dobravaense), Hantaan virus (Hantaan Orthohantavirus), Puumala virus (Orthohantavirus Puumalaense), Seoul virus (Orthohantavirus Seoulense), and Sin Nombre virus (Sin Nombre Orthohantavirus)1. The virus names provided in the source dataset were retained as species labels throughout this study. Each source record was associated with a dataset-specific identifier and one corresponding FASTA sequence record. The identifier consisted solely of a randomly assigned number used within the public dataset and did not correspond to an actual clinical or institutional patient identifier. No directly identifying patient information was available, and the accompanying patient-associated information was anonymous. The dataset included 426 Bayou, 427 Dobrava, 422 Hantaan, 431 Puumala, 435 Seoul, and 430 Sin Nombre records. The source documen­ tation did not provide a sequence-length distribution or specify whether the available viral sequences represented complete genomes, individual genomic segments, or partial sequence fragments. Hantavirus genomes comprise three RNA segments, designated small (S), medium (M), and large (L)1. Nev­ ertheless, the source dataset did not provide S-, M-, or L-segment annotations, genomic coordinates, original sequence-repository information, accession numbers, strain identifiers, or isolate identifiers. Consequently, the specific genomic segment and accession-level provenance of the analyzed sequences could not be determined from the available source information. Furthermore, the dataset did not provide independently verifiable links to the original clinical records or sequence repositories; therefore, the provenance of the patient-associated meta­ data and sequence records could not be independently verified beyond the information supplied with the public dataset38. The accompanying patient-level data included age, sex, geographic region, and sample date. Sample dates for the 2,571 positive records ranged from May 2024 to May 2026. The geographic variable represented the patient’s geographic region rather than the documented geographic origin of the viral sequence or isolate. These patient-level variables were used only for descriptive characterization and were not included as model inputs. The approximately balanced distribution of the six hantavirus classes reflected the composition of the positive records in the source dataset rather than a balancing or subsampling procedure performed in this study. The available source documentation does not indicate whether this distribution was deliberately imposed during construction of the original dataset; therefore, the class frequencies should not be interpreted as representing the natural epi­ demiological prevalence of the six hantavirus species. Before model development, sequence redundancy was systematically assessed to reduce the risk of sequence- level information leakage across evaluation partitions. Exact duplicate sequences were first identified by direct comparison of nucleotide strings. Forty-seven exact-duplicate groups comprised 223 records, corresponding to 176 redundant copies beyond one representative per group. No exact-duplicate group contained conflicting hantavirus species labels. Exact duplicates were retained because they represented distinct source records; nevertheless, identical sequences were constrained to remain within the same sequence-similarity group and, consequently, within the same data partition. Sequence-similarity clustering was subsequently performed using CD-HIT-EST39 at identity thresholds of 99%, 95%, and 90%. CD-HIT-EST was configured using global sequence identity with a minimum alignment coverage of 90% for both the shorter and longer sequences. Word sizes of 10, 10, and 8 were used for the 99%, 95%, and 90% thresholds, respectively. The 99% identity threshold was used to define near-identical sequence groups for the primary leakage-controlled partitioning strategy, whereas the 95% and 90% thresholds were evalu­ ated additionally to characterize broader sequence redundancy. Because the FASTA headers did not provide strain, isolate, accession, outbreak, or lineage identifiers suitable for grouping, the 99%-identity sequence clus­ ters were used as the grouping variable throughout development/test partitioning and cross-validation. Exact duplicates were therefore necessarily contained within the same 99%-identity cluster and could not occur across evaluation boundaries. Hantaviruses are negative-sense RNA viruses; nevertheless, the FASTA sequences were represented using the DNA-style nucleotide alphabet, with thymine (T) rather than uracil (U). Direct examination confirmed that all sequences contained only A, C, G, and T. Consequently, no ambiguous-nucleotide replacement, masking, imputation, sequence exclusion, or U-to-T conversion was required before tokenization. Sequence preprocessing and representation generation were performed using the transformer-based DNA­ BERT-2 model40 with the multimolecule/dnabert2 checkpoint. Previous comparative studies have demonstrated strong sequence-identification performance of DNABERT-2 across diverse genomic datasets, and genome foundation models have also been applied to viral sequence identification35,41. A transformer-based genomic representation approach (DNABERT-2) was used to generate representations for various Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) models. papers.title: DEVELOPMENT OF A PCR TEST SYSTEM FOR THE GENETIC DIAGNOSIS OF HEMORRHAGIC FEVER WITH RENAL SYNDROME
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is an acute zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses. Reliable molecular diagnostics are essential for early detection and epizootiological surveillance. This study aimed to develop and validate a reverse transcription quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR) assay for detection of HFRS-associated orthohantavirus RNA.Species-specific primers (HV P1-F and HV P1-R) and a TaqMan probe (HV P1) targeting the nucleocapsid protein (N) gene within the S segment were designed. A plasmid positive control containing a 242-bp target fragment was constructed. Analytical sensitivity, specificity, reproducibility, and repeatability were evaluated. Field testing included samples from 343 small mammals collected in endemic areas of the West Kazakhstan Region. The assay consistently detected the plasmid control from 1 ng/μL to 1 fg/μL, with Ct values of 37.35 and 37.73 at 1 fg/μL. No specific amplification was observed at 100 ag/μL. A strong linear relationship between Ct values and template concentration was obtained (R2 = 0.998). No false-positive reactions occurred with tick-borne encephalitis virus or Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus RNA. Reproducibility and repeatability showed 100% concordance of qualitative results. HFRS-associated orthohantavirus RNA was detected in 45 of 123 pooled field samples. The minimum infection prevalence was 13.1%, reaching 15.3% in Myodes glareolus and 13.3% in Apodemus uralensis and Microtus arvalis. The developed one-step RT-qPCR assay demonstrated high sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility and is suitable for routine diagnostics and surveillance of natural HFRS foci.

Keywords: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, RT-qPCR, molecular diagnosis, genetic diagnostics, primers, TaqMan probe, validation, hantavirus, orthohantavirus. INTRODUCTION Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains one of the most significant natural focal viral infections in Eurasia, causing tens of thousands of cases annually, partic- ularly in Asian and Eastern European countries [1–6]. Con- temporary climate change, anthropogenic transformation of ecosystems, rodent migration, and urbanization contribute to the expansion of reservoir species ranges, thereby increas- ing the risk of the emergence of new natural foci of the in- fection [7–10]. Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a viral zoonotic natural focal disease characterized by pronounced in- toxication, fever, specific vasculitis accompanied by hemor- rhagic manifestations, and the development of renal inflam- mation with damage to the renal tubules and interstitium, resulting in impaired renal filtration and disruption of fluid and electrolyte homeostasis [11]. HFRS is caused by ortho- hantaviruses belonging to the family Hantaviridae and genus Orthohantavirus [12]. Ortho hantaviruses exhibit consider- able ecological plasticity, a broad range of natural reservoir hosts, and complex patterns of circulation within small-mam- mal populations [13–15]. The genome of orthohantaviruses consists of three seg- ments of negative-sense single-stranded RNA: S, M, and L. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid (N) protein, which binds viral RNA and participates in the formation of the ribo- nucleoprotein complex. N-gene sequences are widely used in the development of molecular assays for the detection of or- thohantaviruses [16–18]. In the Republic of Kazakhstan, official surveillance and registration of HFRS cases have been conducted since 2000, with 302 cases recorded during the period from 2000 to 2024. The disease occurs both as sporadic cases and outbreaks, with pronounced seasonality and a predominance among rural pop- ulations [17, 19–21]. The seasonal peak in hospitalizations oc- curs from November to January, accounting for up to 87.6% of cases, with the highest incidence observed in November. This pattern is associated with the mass migration of rodents into human dwellings and agricultural structures during the cold season. In natural foci, the pathogen is maintained pre- dominantly through circulation within rodent populations, in- cluding Microtus arvalis, Myodes glareolus, Apodemus ural- ensis, and other species [22, 23]. Conventional diagnostic methods for HFRS have substan- tial limitations. Classical virological investigations require propagation of the pathogen in specialized cell lines under BSL-3 containment conditions, which are available only in specialized virological laboratories. This process is labor-in- tensive and does not always yield successful results [24–26]. Serological methods may have insufficient specificity due to cross-reactivity with other orthohantaviruses and tick-borne pathogens and are also predominantly retrospective in nature. IgM antibodies against HFRS-associated viruses generally be- come detectable from 3–4 days after disease onset, whereas IgG antibodies typically appear by days 10–14 [11, 26–28]. In this context, RT-qPCR methods are considered a gold-standard approach for early diagnosis, providing high sensitivity, specificity, and rapid detection of viral RNA [29, 30]. International recommendations from the World Health 176 Eurasian Journal of Applied Biotechnology. No.3, 2026 DOI: 10.11134/btp.3.2026.18 Organization (WHO), the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the MIQE (Minimum In- formation for Publication of Quantitative Real-Time PCR Experiments) guidelines emphasize the need for validated RT-qPCR-based molecular platforms adapted to the genetic diversity and regional characteristics of circulating orthohan- tavirus strains [31–33]. Such approaches provide high ana- lytical sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility under the specific epidemiological and ecological conditions of indi- vidual natural foci. The closest analogue to the proposed test system is the “OM-HFRS-RV” assay (Registration Certificate No. РЗН 2021/15205, dated March 23, 2021, Russian Federation; “OM” product line developed by Syntol) for the detection of hantavirus RNA in biological specimens using real-time PCR. However, this assay has a limitation in that it requires a two- step reaction consisting of reverse transcription followed by amplification of the target RNA fragment. This increases the overall analysis time and reagent consumption [34]. The present study describes the design, development, and comprehensive validation of a novel one-step RT-qPCR test system for the molecular diagnosis of HFRS, including its ap- plication in field studies for the epizootiological surveillance of natural foci in Kazakhstan. The technical outcome of the study is the development of specific oligonucleotides, establishment of positive controls, and detection of HFRS-associated viral RNA using real-time reverse transcription PCR. MATERIALS AND METHODS Oligonucleotide Design and Synthesis An important step in the development of the PCR-based test system was the selection of an appropriate genetic tar- get. A fragment of the N gene located within the S segment of the negative-sense single-stranded RNA genome was se- lected as the target. The target region was selected based on a comparative analysis of S-segment sequences of HFRS-asso- ciated orthohantaviruses available in the GenBank/NCBI da- tabases, taking into account its suitability for primer and hy- drolysis probe design [16, 35]. During oligonucleotide design, multiple sequence align- ment of the N gene was performed. Sequence conservation within the proposed primer- and probe-binding regions, am- plicon length, melting temperatures (Tm), GC content, and the potential for secondary structure formation were evalu- ated. The design process followed the recommendations of the MIQE (Minimum Information for Publication of Quanti- tative Real-Time PCR Experiments) guidelines and aimed to minimize the risk of nonspecific amplification [33, 36, 37]. The specificity of the selected primer and probe sequences was assessed in silico using BLAST and Primer-BLAST by comparison against sequences available in the NCBI Gen- Bank database. Potential homology with non-target viral and bacterial genomes was also evaluated. The analysis revealed no significant sequence matches that could potentially result in nonspecific amplification of the target fragment. The self-complementarity of the oligonucleotides and the potential formation of hairpin structures, homodimers, and heterodimers were additionally assessed using OligoAnalyzer and AutoDimer software. Sequences with unfavorable pre- dicted characteristics were excluded from further experimen- tal evaluation [38, 39]. The following oligonucleotide sequences were selected for the detection of the N gene fragment within the S segment and are presented in Table 1. Oligonucleotide synthesis was performed at the National scientific center for especially dangerous infections (NSCEDI) using standard phosphoramidite chemistry on an H6 auto- mated DNA/RNA synthesizer (K&A Laborgeraete GbR, Ger- many). Phosphoramidites from Glen Research Corporation (USA) and reagents from emp BIOTECH (Germany) were used. Purification of the aqueous primer solutions from syn- thesis by-products was performed using Centri•Pure N10 col- umns (emp BIOTECH GmbH, Germany). The purified aqueous primer solutions were concentrated to dryness using a CentriVap concentrator (Labconco, USA) and subsequently resuspended in deionized water to a final concentration of 100 μM. Primer concentrations were deter- mined using a NanoPhotometer® P-300 spectrophotometer (Implen, Germany). The probes were synthesized by BIGL (Novosibirsk, Russia). The lyophilized probes were reconsti- tuted to a concentration of 100 μM. To assess the diagnostic performance of the assay based on the developed oligonucleotide system, a positive control was constructed using a recombinant plasmid containing the syn- thesized target fragment of the N gene from the S segment of an HFRS-associated orthohantavirus. The nucleotide sequence of the target insert is presented below: GATTGAAGATATTGAGTCACCATCATCGATAT- GGGTTTTTGCTGGAGCACCTGACCGTTGTCCAC- CAACATGCCTATTCATTGCAGGGATTGCTGAACTTG- GAGCATTCTTTTCTATCCTGCAGGACATGCGGAATA- CAATTATGGCCTCAAAGACAGTGGGAACATCT- GAAGAAAAGTTACGAAAGAAATCATCATTCTAT- CAGTCTTATCTCAGGCGAACACAATCAATGGGGA- TACAAC (242 bp). RT-qPCR optimization and amplification conditions RT-qPCR conditions were optimized using the plasmid positive control and a negative control containing deionized water instead of the template. The annealing temperature was determined empirically based on the intensity of the specific amplification signal and the absence of amplification in the negative control. The amplification program is presented in Table 2. Table 1. No.3, 2026 DOI: 10.11134/btp.3.2026.18 RT-qPCR was performed using a Rotor-Gene 6000 re- al-time PCR cycler (Corbett Research, Australia), with fluo- rescence generated by the FAM reporter dye detected in the Green channel. The total reaction volume was 25 μL and con- sisted of 5.0 μL of 5× qPCR reaction mix, 1.0 μL of forward primer (20 pmol/μL), 1.0 μL of reverse primer (20 pmol/μL), 0.5 μL of probe (10 pmol/μL), 5.0 μL of sample RNA, and sterile deionized water to the final volume. The final concen- trations of the primers and probe were 0.8 μM and 0.2 μM, respectively. A run was considered valid when a typical sig- moidal amplification curve was observed for the positive con- trol and no increase in fluorescence signal was detected for the negative control. A sample was considered positive when the amplification curve crossed the predefined threshold within 45 cycles; in the absence of such a curve, the result was in- terpreted as negative. PCR validation To confirm the analytical performance characteristics of the developed reagent kit for the detection of HFRS-asso- ciated orthohantavirus RNA by reverse transcription quan- titative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR), a validation study was performed. The validation study was designed to assess the analytical sensitivity, analytical specificity, reproducibility, and repeatability of the assay. A preliminary assessment of the analytical sensitivity of the PCR component of the test system was performed using serial tenfold dilutions of the plasmid positive control in ac- cordance with established general approaches to the analyti- cal validation of molecular diagnostic methods [40, 41]. The lowest concentration consistently detected across replicates was determined, and the linearity of the relationship between Ct values and the logarithm of template concentration was as- sessed. A statistically validated limit of detection (LoD) for the complete RT-qPCR method was not established within the scope of the present study. Analytical specificity was evaluated using a panel of het- erologous viruses circulating in Kazakhstan, including tick- borne encephalitis virus and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fe- ver virus, in accordance with the requirements for differential diagnosis of natural focal infections. Interlaboratory testing was performed in three structural divisions of the NSCEDI: the Molecular Genetic Research Laboratory, the Laboratory of Natural Focal Viral Infections, and the OBTC-IL. Testing was conducted by different opera- tors on different days using Rotor-Gene 6000 and QuantStu- dio 5 real-time PCR instruments, as well as auxiliary reagents and consumables from different production lots. RNA extraction and field study design RNA was extracted from viral samples and field-mate- rial suspensions using the QIAamp RNA Mini Kit for 250 tests (QIAGEN, Germany), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The extracted RNA samples were subsequently used as templates to assess the specificity of the developed primer set. The field study employed an observational descriptive-an- alytical design. Small mammals were trapped in August–Sep- tember 2025 in HFRS-endemic districts of the West Kazakh- stan Region, including Burlinsky, Shyngyrlau, Terektinsky, and Baiterek districts. Trapping was performed using “Gero” traps baited with standard bread bait and placed at 2-m inter- vals. Species identification was based on morphological char- acteristics. Lung tissue samples were pooled by species and trapping location, resulting in 123 pooled samples derived from 343 individual animals. The minimum infection rate (MIR) was calculated as the number of positive pools divided by the total number of individuals tested and expressed as a percentage. Positive con- trol concentrations ranging from 1 ng/μL to 100 ag/μL were tested. The plasmid DNA concentration was determined us- ing the Quant-iT dsDNA HS Kit (Invitrogen, USA) on a Qu- bit fluorometer (Invitrogen, USA). Each concentration was tested in duplicate. Serial tenfold dilution of the positive plasmid control resulted in a consis- tent increase in Ct values in the Green/FAM channel. Stable detection of the target fragment in both replicates was ob- served over the concentration range from 1 ng/μL to 1 fg/μL. At a concentration of 1 fg/μL, a specific signal was de- tected in both replicates, with Ct values of 37.35 and 37.73, respectively, meeting the predefined criterion for a positive result (Ct ≤38).
