papers.title: Host–Virus Immune Interactions in Andes Virus Infection: Implications for Human-to-Human Transmission, Pathogenesis, and Public Health
papers.abstract: The Andes virus (ANDV, Orthohantavirus, andesense) is unique among hantaviruses in that it may transfer from person to person and cause severe vascular damage. The evidence on host–virus immunological interactions and their importance in disease progression, transmission, and public health is compiled in this narrative review. ANDV mostly affects pulmonary endothelial cells and does not result in widespread cell loss. Rather, the loss of vascular barrier integrity is caused by vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling, Ras homolog family member A (RhoA) activation, breakdown of vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin, hypoxia-related pathways, and mediators produced from infected pericytes. Additionally, the virus interferes with early antiviral defenses involving protein kinase R (PKR), TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1)–interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein (MAVS), and retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)/melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA5). The intensity or outcome of the disease has been associated with increased interleukin-6 (IL-6), altered complement activity, thrombocytopenia, neutralizing-antibody reactions, and specific host genetic variations; nevertheless, significant T-cell activation does not necessarily correspond with viral clearance. Blood and a number of mucosal and secretory samples have been found to contain ANDV ribonucleic acid (RNA), albeit RNA discovery by itself does not prove the presence of an infectious virus. Epidemiological evidence indicates that Secondary transmission is rare and mostly linked to extended close or intimate contact. Genomic sequencing, when paired with epidemiological evidence, can shed light on transmission chains. Recent outbreaks linked to travel further emphasize the significance of worldwide surveillance and coordinated contact tracing. Prospective studies integrating genomic analysis, serial virological sampling, and standardized exposure evaluation are required to more effectively define the infectious phase and transmission patterns

papers.title: Andes virus from the MV Hondius outbreak is highly pathogenic in hamsters and airborne shed
papers.abstract: In May 2026, an outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) caused by Andes virus (ANDV) was detected aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, sparking public health measures in multiple countries. ANDV infections in humans are mostly sporadic, most often linked to exposure to infected rodents in South America, although small clusters of human cases, like the 2026 outbreak on the MV Hondius occur as well. It is not known whether virological factors may contribute to this distinct epidemiology, and no phenotypic characterisation of the newly emerged ANDV (ANDV2026) has been carried out to date. Here, using an ANDV isolate from a presymptomatic patient from the MV Hondius, we studied pathogenesis, identified sites of viral replication, characterized innate and adaptive immune responses, and quantified shedding in golden Syrian hamsters. ANDV2026 proved to be highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe pulmonary disease reminiscent of HPS. ANDV2026 triggered a delayed type-I IFN response and inflammatory response in the lungs consistent with the key pathological features of HPS, and we detected viral replication in both respiratory and extra-respiratory tissues, including the brain. Infected animals mounted neutralising antibodies and T cell responses, the latter directed predominantly against the L and N proteins. Importantly, ANDV2026-infected animals shed virus through multiple routes, and we detected infectious virus in air samplers connected to cages housing ANDV2026-infected hamsters. In contrast, control hamsters infected with a rodent-derived ANDV isolate (ANDV9717869) shed little virus and air samples were consistently negative. These findings consolidate established features of ANDV pathogenesis, while revealing properties not previously described. Phenotypic characterisation of patient-derived ANDV isolates in animal models can strengthen outbreak preparedness, identify markers of disease severity, and support the development of medical countermeasures.

ANDV infections in humans are mostly sporadic, most often linked to exposure to infected rodents in South America, although small clusters of human cases, like the 2026 outbreak on the MV Hondius occur as well. It is not known whether virological factors may contribute to this distinct epidemiology, and no phenotypic characterisation of the newly emerged ANDV (ANDV2026) has been carried out to date. Here, using an ANDV isolate from a presymptomatic patient from the MV Hondius, we studied pathogenesis, identified sites of viral replication, characterized innate and adaptive immune responses, and quantified shedding in golden Syrian hamsters. ANDV2026 proved to be highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe pulmonary disease reminiscent of HPS. ANDV2026 triggered a delayed type-I IFN response and inflammatory response in the lungs consistent with the key pathological features of HPS, and we detected viral replication in both respiratory and extra-respiratory tissues, including the brain. Infected animals mounted neutralising antibodies and T cell responses, the latter directed predominantly against the L and N proteins. Importantly, ANDV2026-infected animals shed virus through multiple routes, and we detected infectious virus in air samplers connected to cages housing ANDV2026-infected hamsters. In contrast, control hamsters infected with a rodent-derived ANDV isolate (ANDV9717869) shed little virus and air samples were consistently negative. These findings consolidate established features of ANDV pathogenesis, while revealing properties not previously described. Phenotypic characterisation of patient-derived ANDV isolates in animal models can strengthen outbreak preparedness, identify markers of disease severity, and support the development of medical countermeasures.

Phenotypic characterization of patient-derived ANDV isolates in animal 44 models can strengthen outbreak preparedness, identify markers of disease severity, and support 45 the development of medical countermeasures. 46 3 | P a g e INTRODUCTION 47 On the 2nd of May 2026, a cluster of severe respiratory disease aboard the Dutch cruise ship MV 48 Hondius was notified to the World Health organization (WHO)1-3. Soon after, ANDV was 49 diagnosed as the cause of the outbreak, which overall led to 13 reported cases, including three 50 deaths4. Confirmed cases were all aboard the MV Hondius, although the outbreak led to 51 monitoring of 653 individuals in 33 countries around the globe. 52 ANDV is classified within the family Orthohantaviridae5-8. These are viruses that cause two distinct 53 disease complexes: the hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Europe and Asia, and 54 the hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas, caused among others by Sin Nombre 55 virus (SNV) and Andes virus (ANDV), respectively9. HPS is usually presents in four distinct clinical 56 phases: febrile, cardiopulmonary, diuretic and convalescent10,11. Most cases are characterized by 57 pulmonary edema driven by increased vascular permeability, terminally leading to cardiogenic 58 shock and death12. The case fatality rate of the MV Hondius outbreak was 23%, lower than for 59 previously reported ANDV clusters. Direct comparison is difficult however, due to the relatively 60 low number of cases in this outbreak and early access to medical care for many of the individuals 61 affected13-15. 62 ANDV is endemic in Southern Argentina and Chile, where it causes seasonal outbreaks every 63 year9,16. Humans are believed to become infected mostly after exposure to aerosolized infectious 64 excretions of the rodent reservoir, the long-tailed rice rat (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus)5,6,17. 65 Andes virus (ANDV) was first detected in 1995, when it caused an outbreak of 16 cases and nine 66 deaths18. This outbreak and subsequent ones suggested that ANDV can be capable of human- 67 to-human transmission, with the main risk factor being in close contact with infected individuals in 68 enclosed settings18,19. Some cases have also been described without any documented direct 69 contact, hinting at a respiratory transmission route, though available data cannot distinguish 70 airborne shedding of infectious virus from contamination of the surrounding environment20. On 71 the MV Hondius, patients were in direct contact with each other, suggesting ANDV human-to- 72 4 | P a g e human transmission. One potential asymptomatic case of ANDV infection in a health-care worker 73 with low-level viraemia was also reported, despite only indirect exposure21-23. 74 Few studies have phenotyped ANDV isolates obtained directly from human patients21-23, and 75 fewer still have done so in vivo to define key viral characteristics such as virulence and host 76 responses22,24. This reflects the sporadic nature of HPS and its restricted geographical distribution. 77 ANDV is also notoriously difficult to isolate, as infection is typically diagnosed once patients have 78 already developed neutralizing antibodies. As a result, our understanding of the biological 79 differences between ANDV isolates associated with different cases and outbreaks is incomplete. 80 Here, we characterized the ANDV isolate associated with the MV Hondius outbreak 81 (ANDV/2026/hondius-NL-12, henceforth ANDV2026). Using the golden Syrian hamster model, we 82 studied viral pathogenesis, replication sites, and the host innate and adaptive immune responses. 83 We also analyzed virus shedding from infected animals and sampled air from the cages of infected 84 hamsters for ANDV RNA and infectious virus. Throughout our study, the human isolate ANDV2026 85 was compared with a rodent-derived ANDV strain (ANDV9717869). Altogether, in vivo phenotyping 86 contributes to the continuous risk assessment of emerging viruses of global health concern. 87 88 RESULTS 89 90 ANDV2026 causes severe, systemic infection in hamsters. Golden Syrian hamsters were 91 intranasally inoculated with a low dose (200 TCID50/hamster) of either ANDV2026 (n=18) or 92 ANDV9717869 (n=18). ANDV2026 was isolated from whole-blood sample collected from a pre- 93 symptomatic patient during the 2026 ANDV outbreak linked to the cruise ship MV Hondius3. 94 Backtitration of the inocula revealed that the animals received a dose of 28 TCID50 of ANDV2026 95 and 89 TCID50 of ANDV9717869. Six animals per group were sacrificed at 3, 7 and 14 days post- 96 inoculation (dpi), or earlier when reaching humane endpoints. Sixty percent of the hamsters 97 inoculated with ANDV2026 reached the humane endpoint between 12 and 14 dpi (Fig 1a). 98 5 | P a g e Symptoms included lethargy, ruffled fur, decreased mobility, and severe respiratory distress. In 99 general, animals reached humane endpoints within 24-72 hours after the onset of symptoms. The 100 development of clinical symptoms was also accompanied by a loss of body weight of up to 9% in 101 three days (Fig. 1b). At the terminal stage of the experiment (12-14 dpi), the lung-to-bodyweight 102 ratio of ANDV2026 inoculated animals was significantly increased when compared to both mock- 103 and ANDV9717869-inoculated animals (Fig. 1c). These values reflected the macroscopic lung 104 lesions observed in ANDV2026 inoculated animals, characterized by increased size, rounded edges 105 and darkened color with severe, diffuse lung oedema (Fig. 1d), as described previously for severe 106 ANDV infections in hamsters25-27. 107 Next, we tested 15 respiratory and non-respiratory tissues for presence of both viral RNA by qRT- 108 PCR and infectious virus by titration (Fig. 1e,f). At the early timepoints (3 dpi), viral RNA and 109 infectious virus were only detected in the nasal turbinates with titers essentially identical in both 110 ANDV2026- and ANDV9717869-inoculated animals. At 7 and 12-14 dpi all tissues contained both viral 111 RNA and infectious virus with titers in most cases higher in ANDV2026-infected animals. 112 Interestingly, we observed no significant differences in viral loads in myocardium and liver 113 between ANDV2026- and ANDV9717869-infected hamsters 12-14 dpi. These tissues were previously 114 reported as the prime targets of virus replication in ANDV9717869-infected hamsters26. We observed 115 the highest viral titers in the respiratory tract (nasal turbinates and lungs), submandibular salivary 116 glands, pancreas, and adrenal glands collected from ANDV2026-infected animals. 117 Sites of ANDV replication. Next, we investigated the sites of viral replication using 118 immunohistochemistry (IHC) and RNA in situ-hybridisation (ISH) in formalin-fixed and paraffin 119 embedded samples from inoculated animals. In the lungs, we detected abundant viral RNA (Fig. 120 2a) and protein in ANDV2026-infected animals at 7dpi, with widespread distribution in the 121 parenchyma. Quantification of RNA signal showed virus spread in wider areas of the lungs in 122 ANDV2026-infected hamsters compared to those infected with ANDV9717869 (Fig. 2b-c), both at 7 123 and 14 dpi. Virus RNA was detectable, both by qualitative assessment of the histological sections 124 6 | P a g e and by software-assisted image analysis28, in the lung parenchyma and endothelial cells, but not 125 in the bronchial epithelium of all ANDV infected animals at both 7 and 14 dpi (Fig. 2c-d). As 126 expected, extrarespiratory organs such as liver, kidney, myocardium, and many others showed 127 abundant viral RNA signal in endothelial cells, while epithelial cells were viral RNA negative (Fig. 128 2e). Importantly, we also detected ANDV2026 widely distributed in the brain, including in endothelial 129 cells of blood vessels, meninges and neurons (Fig. 2e and Fig. S1). 130 The widespread infection of endothelial cells throughout all organs was not accompanied by 131 severe histopathological lesions in both groups of animals. Serum chemistry revealed reduced 132 total protein and albumin concentrations in ANDV2026-infected hamsters compared to ANDV9717869- 133 and mock-infected animals, consistent with endothelial dysfunction and leakage of proteins to the 134 extravascular space (Fig. 2f). We found moderately abnormal values for alkaline phosphatase, 135 alanine-aminotransferase, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine and phosphorus in ANDV2026-infected 136 animals (in the terminal stages of the disease), consistent with kidney and liver damage, although 137 major histopathological lesions were not observed (Fig. 2f, Fig. S2). Serum values of amylase, 138 calcium, glucose, sodium and total bilirubin remained similar between groups (Fig. S2). 139 Lung pathology in ANDV2026-infected hamsters correlates with preferential activation of the 140 type I IFN response. At the latest stages of disease, we detected histopathological lesions 141 throughout the lungs in hamsters infected with ANDV2026, similar to severe HPS previously 142 described in this model 25-27. Lesions include diffuse alveolar damage, multifocal, 143 lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, alveolar histiocytosis, alveolar oedema, leukocytolastic vasculitis, 144 perivascular oedema, sloughing of bronchial epithelial cells to various degrees and hemorrhages 145 in the vessel (Fig. 3a-b). We also detected fibrin accumulation in damaged alveoli in more severe 146 cases (Fig. 3b, middle panel). Infiltrates of both B-cells (Pax+ cells) and macrophage (Iba-1+ cells) 147 infiltrates, but not T-cells (CD3+), were observed in the lungs of ANDV2026-infected animals (Fig. 148 3c-d). 149 7 | P a g e In addition, activation of the type I IFN response (henceforth IFN), assessed by the upregulation 150 of the IFN-stimulated gene Mx-1, was evident in the lungs of both ANDV2026- and ANDV9217869- 151 infected animals (Fig. 3d, last column). We detected relatively little Mx-1 at 7 dpi despite the 152 presence of abundant virus replication. This observation reinforces the concept that ANDV is able 153 to evade recognition by the host IFN response for some time. 154 Because ANDV, both in humans and in hamsters, causes primarily a pulmonary disease, we 155 further investigated whether the levels of the IFN response vary between lungs and other organs 156 (Fig. 4). To this end, we quantified the expression of IFIT-1 RNA, another interferon stimulated 157 gene (ISG), in FFPE sections of lungs, spleen, myocardium, kidney and liver of ANDV2026-infected 158 animals by RNAscope and normalized the data in relation to the presence of viral RNA in each of 159 these organs. We found the highest relative expression of IFIT-1 RNA in the lungs, followed by 160 the spleen (Fig. 4). These data are in line with the relatively upregulation of proinflammatory 161 genes such as CXCL10 that we detected in these two organs (Fig. S3). Of note, we did find 162 bronchial epithelial cells expressing ISGs in the absence of viral replication (Fig. 4a), most likely 163 triggered by an IFN response in infected neighboring cells. The IFN and inflammatory response 164 in respiratory epithelia may explain the lesions (sloughed off cells) observed in some of these 165 animals. 166 Combined, ANDV2026 causes a disease comparable to HPS in hamsters, characterized 167 predominantly by lung pathology, endothelial cell dysfunction, with a relatively long incubation 168 period where abundant virus replication does not trigger a detectable inflammatory response. 169 Adaptive immune response to ANDV in experimentally inoculated hamsters. We next 170 assessed antibody and T-cell responses in ANDV-infected animals. We detected neutralizing 171 antibodies only at 12-14 dpi in sera from animals infected with either ANDV9717869 or ANDV2026. 172 The mean VNT50 did not differ significantly between groups, even though all ANDV2026-infected 173 animals mounted a response compared to 40% of the ANDV9717689-infected animals (Fig. 5a). To 174 further characterize the ANDV-specific adaptive immune response, we isolated lymphocytes from 175 8 | P a g e hamster lungs at both 7 and 14 dpi and stimulated them with overlapping peptide pools covering 176 the N, Gn, Gc, and L proteins (the latter split in four distinct pools, L1-4) (Fig. 5b). At 7 dpi, antigen- 177 specific T-cell responses were limited in all groups (Fig. 5d). However, strong antigen-specific T- 178 cell responses were detected at 12-14 dpi regardless of group. The majority of virus-specific T- 179 cells targeted the L-protein (Fig. 5c, Fig. S4); these were comparable between ANDV9717869- and 180 ANDV2026-inoculated hamsters, and higher than those observed in mock-inoculated animals, 181 although significance was reached only for ANDV9717869 (Fig. 5e). N-specific T-cell responses 182 were higher in ANDV9717869-inoculated animals than in ANDV2026- and mock-inoculated animals at 183 12-14 dpi (Fig. 5e). Similar responses were observed with lymphocytes isolated from the spleen, 184 although the background in mock-inoculated hamsters was higher, complicating data 185 interpretation (Fig. S4). 186 Infectious virus is shed in the air by ANDV2026-infected animals. The ANDV outbreak aboard 187 the MV Hondius raised questions about the potential of increased shedding, and hence increased 188 transmissibility, of ANDV. In hamsters, we detected viral genomes (Fig. 6a) and infectious virus 189 (Fig. S5) in throat swabs of all ANDV2026-inoculated animals from 7 dpi onwards, with 190 progressively increasing titers until the end of the experiment (Fig. 6a). We detected infectious 191 virus in only one ANDV9717869-infected animal. By immunohistochemistry, we detected numerous 192 clusters of ANDV2026 infected endothelial cells, olfactory epithelium, degenerated and sloughing 193 olfactory epithelium, as well as the ducts of the nasal submucosal glands of the olfactory portion 194 of the turbinates, especially at 14 dpi. Only very few cells of the respiratory epithelium showed 195 occasionally virus positive signal (Fig. 6d-f). ANDV9717869-inoculated animals displayed only 196 occasional virus-positive cells in the nasal turbinates (either endothelial cells, cells within the 197 olfactory epithelium, or the submucosal glands). 198 We also detected ANDV2026 RNA in urine collected at study endpoints, but volumes were too small 199 to test for presence of infectious virus. Furthermore, we detected both viral RNA and infectious 200 9 | P a g e virus in feces homogenates collected from cages housing ANDV2026 infected animals (Fig. 6c and 201 S5). 202 Hence, ANDV2026-infected animals shed infectious virus from the respirat…

analysis.background: An outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome caused by Andes virus (ANDV) was detected aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius in May 2026, highlighting the need for phenotypic characterization of the newly emerged ANDV2026 strain.
analysis.methods: An ANDV isolate from a presymptomatic patient was used to study pathogenesis, viral replication sites, innate and adaptive immune responses, and shedding in golden Syrian hamsters.
analysis.results: ANDV2026 was highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe pulmonary disease, delayed type‑I IFN and inflammatory responses, and viral replication in respiratory and extra‑respiratory tissues including the brain. Infected animals mounted neutralizing antibodies and T‑cell responses mainly against L and N proteins, and shed virus through multiple routes; infectious virus was detected in air samplers. In contrast, a rodent‑derived ANDV9717869 isolate shed little virus and air samples were negative.

analysis.summary_en: Background: An outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome caused by Andes virus (ANDV) was detected aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius in May 2026, highlighting the need for phenotypic characterization of the newly emerged ANDV2026 strain. Methods: An ANDV isolate from a presymptomatic patient was used to study pathogenesis, viral replication sites, innate and adaptive immune responses, and shedding in golden Syrian hamsters. Results: ANDV2026 was highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe pulmonary disease, delayed type‑I IFN and inflammatory responses, and viral replication in respiratory and extra‑respiratory tissues including the brain. Infected animals mounted neutralizing antibodies and T‑cell responses mainly against L and N proteins, and shed virus through multiple routes; infectious virus was detected in air samplers. In contrast, a rodent‑derived ANDV9717869 isolate shed little virus and air samples were negative. Contribution: The study consolidates established ANDV pathogenesis features while revealing previously undescribed airborne shedding, thereby strengthening outbreak preparedness, identifying disease‑severity markers, and supporting medical countermeasure development. Limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

papers.title: Design and in silico evaluation of PV-GNProtecta: an mRNA multi-epitope vaccine candidate against Puumala virus using immunoinformatics and structural analysis.
papers.abstract: Abstract Puumala virus (PUUV), the principal causative agent of nephropathia epidemica (NE), poses a significant public health threat due to its zoonotic transmission, renal complications, and the lack of an approved vaccine. In this study, an immunoinformatics-driven mRNA multi-epitope vaccine, PV-GNProtecta, was designed using conserved regions of the viral glycoprotein (G) and nucleoprotein (N). Highly antigenic, non-allergenic, and non-toxic T-cell and B-cell epitopes were identified and assembled with appropriate adjuvants to enhance immunogenicity. Population coverage analysis suggested broad HLA responsiveness across diverse populations. The vaccine construct exhibited favorable physicochemical properties, including stability, solubility, and antigenicity. Structural validation predicted high model quality, with 95.5% of residues located in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 91.4. Molecular docking and MM-GBSA analyses predicted favorable computational interactions between PV-GNProtecta and TLR4, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation provided computational insights into the dynamic behavior of the vaccine-TLR4 complex. Codon optimization suggested compatibility of the designed sequence with an Escherichia coli -based expression framework. Immune simulation predicted potential humoral and cellular immune response patterns, including changes in IgG, IFN-γ, and IL-2 levels. The designed mRNA sequence exhibited favorable predicted secondary structural characteristics; however, further experimental evaluation is required to assess translational efficiency and stability. Although this study is limited to computational analyses and requires experimental validation, the findings suggest that PV-GNProtecta may represent a potential candidate for further investigation against PUUV infection.

PUUV infection presents with highly variable outcomes, ranging from subclinical cases (70–80%) to severe HFRS, and carries a fatality rate of about 0.1%. PUUV infection commonly presents with sudden fever, headache, back pain, nausea, gastrointestinal symptoms, thrombocytopenia, hematuria, and varying degrees of acute kidney impairment. In some patients, additional manifestations such as blurred vision, dizziness, insomnia, respiratory complications, oliguria, and subsequent polyuria during recovery may also occur. Although PUUV infection is generally considered mild, severe complications can occur in a subset of patients, including acute kidney failure, hypotension, shock, pulmonary edema, Guillain-Barré syndrome, respiratory distress, disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC), myocarditis, encephalitis, pituitary hemorrhage, seizures, and, in rare cases, multiorgan failure or fatal cerebral hemorrhage. The first identification of PUUV occurred in the early 1980s when the virus was isolated from bank voles (Myodes glareolus) in the Puumala region of Finland. Between July 1989 and June 1996, Finland reported 6701 PUUV infection cases confirmed via serological assays, with the highest incidence in the Itä-Savo district and a mortality rate below 0.1%, and later from 1995 to 2008, 22,681 cases were recorded with an average annual incidence of 31 per 100,000 population, resulting in 13 deaths and 52% of patients requiring hospitalization. PUUV accounts for approximately 93% of all notified hantavirus infections in Germany and caused a major outbreak in 2007 in Baden-Württemberg with 1089 reported human cases, while the highest annual number of PUUV infections in Germany was recorded in 2010 since hantavirus surveillance began in 2001. Also in 2007, Sweden’s Västerbotten County experienced a surprisingly severe outbreak of PUUV infection, with NE rates hitting 313 cases per 100,000 residents. Between 2001 and 2017, a total of 12,148 hantavirus disease cases were recorded, of which 9714 (approximately 97.41%) were attributed to PUUV infection. In 2019, Europe recorded over 4000 hantavirus cases (0.8 per 100,000), 98% caused by PUUV, with Finland and Germany making up 69% of the total. From 2018 to 2025, Hungary recorded 51 lab-confirmed hantavirus infections, 20 of which were specifically linked to the PUUV. In Finland, between 560 and 3800 cases of NE are reported each year, though the actual number is believed to be nearly six times higher. PUUV is a spherical enveloped pathogen characterized by a segmented negative-sense single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) genome. The PUUV possesses a tripartite genome: the L segment (~ 6.5 kb) encodes a ~ 2156-amino-acid L protein (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase) with replicase, transcriptase, and endonuclease functions; the M segment (~ 3.7 kb) encodes a ~ 1148-amino-acid glycoprotein precursor that is co-translationally cleaved into Gn (70 kDa) and Gc (55 kDa); and the S segment (~ 1.8 kb) encodes a ~ 433-amino-acid nucleocapsid (N) protein. Gc is the protein that mediates fusion by the identification of a peptide of fusion, whereas Gn serves as a folding chaperone for Gc and controls the time of fusion; both are necessary for the virus to adhere as well as enter host cells. Gn and Gc form the principal antigenic surface of PUUV and are major targets of neutralizing antibodies, contributing to protective immunity and vaccine relevance. The N protein plays multiple roles in viral genome transport, replication, and assembly through its interactions with host cellular proteins, while also acting as a highly immunogenic viral component in both humans and animal models. The N protein is highly conserved among orthohantaviruses and elicits a strong early antibody response during acute infection, making it an important target for both diagnostic applications and vaccine development. Various vaccine platforms are available, each possessing distinct advantages and drawbacks. For example, live attenuated vaccines trigger strong, long-lasting immunity but can be risky for immunocompromised individuals due to possible reversion to virulence; inactivated vaccines are safer and more stable, though they usually require multiple doses; subunit vaccines use only key antigens, lowering the chance of side effects, but often need adjuvants and booster shots to achieve durable protection. Moreover, DNA vaccines offer rapid, stable, and cost-effective production with long-lasting immunity, but they often show weak immunogenicity in humans and face delivery challenges. In contrast, the key advantage of mRNA vaccines lies in their rapid design and production, enabling swift responses to emerging infections and pandemic threats without the need to culture live pathogens. In recognition of these advances, the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine honored Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman for their groundbreaking contributions to nucleoside engineering, a key innovation that enabled the successful development of mRNA vaccines against COVID-19. Recent developments in bioinformatics have improved biopharmaceutical design by enabling rapid prediction of protein features, structural modeling, and immunogenicity assessment. These computational approaches accelerate the identification and optimization of therapeutic candidates while reducing time and experimental costs; however, challenges related to prediction accuracy, biological complexity, and the need for experimental validation remain important considerations. Reverse vaccinology (RV) applies bioinformatics and immunoinformatics to screen microbial genomes for conserved, immunogenic epitopes, enabling faster, safer, and cost-effective vaccine development compared to traditional pathogen culturing, a slow and labor-intensive process. Vaccine development against PUUV infection has included inactivated whole-virus vaccines, recombinant subunit vaccines, virus-like particle (VLP)-based approaches, and DNA vaccines. Among these, inactivated and DNA vaccine candidates have demonstrated promising immunogenicity in preclinical studies. Currently, no vaccine has been authorized by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for PUUV infection. Several studies have suggested the potential of multi-epitope vaccine approaches using immunoinformatics-based strategies. Khan et al. developed a multi-epitope vaccine candidate against SARS-CoV-2 by integrating epitope prediction, antigenicity assessment, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and immune response analysis, demonstrating the feasibility of computational vaccine design approaches. Similarly, Peele et al. designed a multi-epitope vaccine construct containing predicted B-cell and T-cell epitopes and evaluated its structural and immunological properties through computational analyses. These studies highlighted the potential of combining multiple immune targets within a single vaccine construct; however, their findings remained primarily dependent on computational predictions and required experimental validation to confirm immunogenicity and protective efficacy. However, despite these advances, several challenges remain in current multi-epitope vaccine development strategies. Computational vaccine designs are dependent on prediction algorithms, reference databases, structural modeling assumptions, and available biological information, which may influence the reliability of predicted vaccine candidates. In addition, variations in epitope selection criteria, antigen conservation analysis, population coverage evaluation, and structural validation approaches can affect the effectiveness of computational vaccine design. Recent studies have emphasized that although immunoinformatics approaches accelerate multi-epitope vaccine development, comprehensive experimental validation remains essential for confirming biological relevance and protective potential. Despite previous vaccine development efforts, including inactivated whole-virus vaccines, recombinant subunit vaccines, virus-like particle (VLP)-based approaches, and DNA vaccine candidates, no PUUV vaccine has currently received regulatory approval. An integrated mRNA multi-epitope vaccine strategy targeting conserved regions of both PUUV glycoproteins (Gn/Gc) and nucleocapsid protein remains insufficiently explored. A comprehensive framework combining conserved antigen identification, multi-epitope vaccine construction, structural evaluation, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and immune response prediction for PUUV has not been extensively investigated. Therefore, this study aimed to design and evaluate the PV-GNProtecta vaccine candidate using an integrated immunoinformatics workflow involving conserved antigen identification, epitope prediction, structural modeling, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and immune response prediction. The findings provide computational insights into the potential characteristics of PV-GNProtecta while recognizing the necessity of experimental validation for future assessment. Materials and methods Acquisition and characterization of viral protein sequences The UniProt protein database (https://www.uniprot.org/; accessed on 15 July 2025) was used for obtaining amino acid sequences of the target proteins from PUUV of G (accession number: P41266) and N (accession numbers: P41270). The G and N proteins were selected due to their key roles in PUUV infection and immune recognition. The G protein mediates viral attachment and entry and is a major target of neutralizing antibodies, whereas the highly conserved N protein contributes to viral replication and induces strong immune responses. Compared with the intracellular RdRp/L protein, G and N provide more suitable targets for antibody and cellular immune responses. A comparative evaluation of these proteins is provided in Supplementary Table S14. Physicochemical and structural characterization of selected proteins The selected PUUV G and N proteins were characterized for signal peptide presence, transmembrane regions, and subcellular localization. Signal peptide prediction was performed using SignalP 6.0 (https://services.healthtech.dtu.dk/services/SignalP-6.0/; accessed on 15 September 2026) with the organism group selected as Eukarya and the default prediction model. Transmembrane topology was predicted using DeepTMHMM version 1.0.57 (accessed on 15 September 2026) using the default settings. Subcellular localization information was obtained from UniProt (https://www.uniprot.org/; accessed on 15 September 2026) based on available curated annotations. Analysis of multiple sequence alignment and evolutionary relationships To support RV analysis, the sequence is encoded using amino acid residue codes and preserved as a FASTA sequence file. The acquired sequences were subsequently utilized for multiple sequence alignment (MSA) through the Clustal Omega platform (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/jdispatcher/msa/clustalo; accessed on 05 August 2025). The Mega X tool (https://www.megasoftware.net/; accessed on 05 August 2025) was employed for phylogenetic analysis on both genomes. Prediction of epitopes for MHC I, MHC II, and linear B-cell interactions The MHC I epitopes from the G and N proteins were found using the Immune Epitope Database (IEDB) (http://tools.iedb.org/mhci/; accessed on 20 August 2025) software, with a percentile rank < 1.00 as the selection criterion. This tool is a sophisticated database comprising information on MHC molecules, T-cell and B-cell epitopes, antibodies, and MHC-binding ligands identified in humans and various animal taxonomic groups, including primates and rodents. A cutoff percentile rank of less than 1.00 was implemented for epitope selection, which suggests that the binding affinity was improved. Lower percentile rank values indicate stronger predicted peptide–MHC binding affinity. The IEDB (http://tools.iedb.org/mhcii/; accessed on 20 August 2025) was applied to forecast the MHC II epitopes inside the designated areas of these proteins, and peptides with percentile ranks < 1.00 were considered potential high-affinity binders and selected for further evaluation. Subsequently, the human allele reference sets were employed to predict CD8 + and CD4 + binding. The ABCpred tool (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/abcpred/; accessed on 25 August 2025) was used to estimate the continuous B-cell epitopes of the selected portions of these proteins. This tool provides epitope predictions by analyzing the sequence features of the target antigens. This program uses an affinity scale method based on a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to predict continuous B-cell epitopes. Additionally, the MHC-II epitopes underwent some additional analyses, including IL-10 (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/il10pred/; accessed on 25 September 2026), IFN-gamma (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/ifnepitope/predict.php; accessed on 25 September 2026), IL-2 (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/il2pred/; accessed on 25 September 2026) and IL-4 (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/il4pred/design.php; accessed on 25 September 2026) by using the respective servers. Linear B-cell epitopes were forecasted with ABCpred with a standard window length of 16 amino acids and a score cutoff of 0.51. Antigenicity was evaluated using the VaxiJen v2.0 (https://www.ddg-pharmfac.net/vaxijen/VaxiJen/VaxiJen.html; accessed on 28 August 2025) server under the viral protein model with the default threshold value of 0.4. Peptides with antigenicity scores ≥ 0.4 were considered probable antigens and retained for further analysis, whereas those scoring below this threshold were excluded. The threshold value of 0.4 was selected based on the default classification cutoff recommended for the VaxiJen viral model, which was established through performance evaluation of the prediction system. AllerTOP v2.1 (threshold: 0.5) (https://www.ddg-pharmfac.net/allertop_test/; accessed on 28 August 2025) and ToxinPred (threshold: 0.0) servers (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/toxinpred/algo.php; accessed on 28 August 2025) were deployed in order to make predictions on allergenicity and toxicity, respectively. The allergenicity was evaluated utilizing AllerTOP v2.1 with the server's standard ACC/k-NN algorithm configurations. Also, toxicity prediction was performed using the ToxinPred server with the SVM (Swiss-Prot)-based prediction method, applying the default threshold value of 0.0 and a window length of 17 residues. Peptides were classified according to the server-generated SVM prediction score, and sequences predicted as toxic were excluded, whereas non-toxic peptides were retained for further analysis. All settings were preserved according to the server’s default configuration. The selected epitopes were not chosen based only on prediction scores; additional analyses, including antigenicity, safety assessment, sequence conservation, population coverage, and MHC interaction evaluation, were also considered to improve the reliability of epitope selection. Evaluation of population-level coverage The prevalence of HLA alleles varies across different geographies and ethnic communities. The population coverage of the chosen T-cell epitopes was assessed via the IEDB Population Coverage tool (http://tools.iedb.org/pop…

full_text_sections.full_text: Design and in silico evaluation of PV-GNProtecta: an mRNA multi-epitope vaccine candidate against Puumala virus using immunoinformatics and structural analysis Puumala virus (PUUV), the principal causative agent of nephropathia epidemica (NE), poses a significant public health threat due to its zoonotic transmission, renal complications, and the lack of an approved vaccine. In this study, an immunoinformatics-driven mRNA multi-epitope vaccine, PV-GNProtecta, was designed using conserved regions of the viral glycoprotein (G) and nucleoprotein (N). Highly antigenic, non-allergenic, and non-toxic T-cell and B-cell epitopes were identified and assembled with appropriate adjuvants to enhance immunogenicity. Population coverage analysis suggested broad HLA responsiveness across diverse populations. The vaccine construct exhibited favorable physicochemical properties, including stability, solubility, and antigenicity. Structural validation predicted high model quality, with 95.5% of residues located in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 91.4. Molecular docking and MM-GBSA analyses predicted favorable computational interactions between PV-GNProtecta and TLR4, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation provided computational insights into the dynamic behavior of the vaccine-TLR4 complex. Codon optimization suggested compatibility of the designed sequence with an Escherichia coli-based expression framework. Immune simulation predicted potential humoral and cellular immune response patterns, including changes in IgG, IFN-γ, and IL-2 levels. The designed mRNA sequence exhibited favorable predicted secondary structural characteristics; however, further experimental evaluation is required to assess translational efficiency and stability. Although this study is limited to computational analyses and requires experimental validation, the findings suggest that PV-GNProtecta may represent a potential candidate for further investigation against PUUV infection. analysis.background: Puumala virus (PUUV) is the main cause of nephropathia epidemica, a zoonotic disease with renal complications and no approved vaccine, representing a public‑health concern.
analysis.methods: An immunoinformatics pipeline was used to design an mRNA multi‑epitope vaccine (PV‑GNProtecta) from conserved glycoprotein (G) and nucleoprotein (N) regions; epitopes were screened for high antigenicity, non‑allergenicity and non‑toxicity, assembled with adjuvants, and evaluated for population HLA coverage, physicochemical properties, structural quality (95.5% Ramachandran favored, ERRAT 91.4), molecular docking and 100 ns MD with TLR4, codon optimization for E. coli expression, and immune‑simulation of IgG, IFN‑γ and IL‑2 responses.
analysis.results: The construct contained highly antigenic, non‑allergenic, non‑toxic T‑ and B‑cell epitopes, showed broad HLA coverage, favorable stability, solubility and antigenicity, high structural model quality, predicted strong TLR4 binding with stable dynamics, compatible codon usage for bacterial expression, and simulated humoral and cellular immune activation.
analysis.contribution: The in silico data suggest PV‑GNProtecta as a potential vaccine candidate warranting experimental validation against PUUV infection.
analysis.limitations: Findings are limited to computational predictions; experimental studies are needed to confirm translational efficiency, stability, and immunogenicity.

analysis.summary_en: Background: PUUV causes nephropathia epidemica and lacks a vaccine, posing a public‑health threat. Methods: An immunoinformatics workflow designed an mRNA multi‑epitope vaccine from conserved G and N regions, selecting antigenic, non‑allergenic, non‑toxic epitopes, assessing HLA coverage, physicochemical and structural quality, docking and MD with TLR4, codon optimization, and immune simulation. Results: The construct showed broad HLA responsiveness, favorable stability and solubility, 95.5% Ramachandran‑favored residues, ERRAT 91.4, strong predicted TLR4 interaction, stable dynamics, and simulated IgG, IFN‑γ, IL‑2 responses. Contribution: PV‑GNProtecta emerges as a promising candidate for further experimental testing against PUUV. Limitations: All results are computational; experimental validation of expression, stability and immunogenicity is required.

papers.title: Hantavirus in Dentistry: Occupational Exposure Considerations and a Proposed Tiered Infection Prevention and Control Framework-A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Objective The aim of this study is to synthesize evidence on hantavirus transmission and occupational exposure pathways relevant to dentistry, and to propose an evidence-informed tiered infection prevention and control (IPC) framework that distinguishes established from theoretical risk. Material and methods The initial narrative search covered database inception through May 15, 2026 in MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, and WHO/CDC/ECDC/OSHA sources, followed by a targeted PubMed/MEDLINE and public-health guidance update through August 18, 2026. Approximately 1450 records were identified. After duplicate removal, 1070 records were subjected to title/abstract screening, 215 full-text records were assessed for eligibility, and 45 sources were included in the final synthesis, comprising 34 peer-reviewed publications and 11 gray-literature or public-health guidance sources. Results Environmental exposure to infected-rodent contamination is the established occupational pathway. Limited person-to-person transmission is documented for the Andes virus (ANDV), but no dental transmission has been reported. ANDV RNA and culture-based infectivity have been demonstrated in some oral/respiratory fluids; however, dental-aerosol transmission has not been shown. Dental-specific occupational risk therefore remains unquantified. Conclusions No dental transmission has been documented, and patient-related risk remains uncertain. Standard precautions and rodent control are foundational; suspected or confirmed ANDV warrants transmission-based precautions and airborne precautions for aerosol-generating procedures according to current guidance. The proposed dental tiers are evidence-informed, author-derived, and unvalidated.

papers.title: DNA and mRNA Vaccines Against Hantaviruses: Antigen Design, Delivery Strategies and Translational Progress.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are members of the Hantaviridae family, which can cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). At present, no specific antiviral treatment is available for hantavirus infection, while licensed hantavirus vaccines are restricted to a limited number of countries in Asia. This review summarizes recent advances in hantavirus deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines, focusing on antigen design, delivery systems, immunogenicity, safety and translational development. Peer-reviewed studies published primarily within the past 10 years were evaluated together with available hantavirus vaccine trials registered in ClinicalTrials.gov, with emphasis on Hantaan virus (HTNV), Puumala virus (PUUV) and Andes virus (ANDV). DNA vaccine candidates have demonstrated immunogenicity in preclinical and early clinical studies, with an acceptable safety profile. mRNA vaccines represent a newer approach with promising preclinical evidence of humoral and cellular immune responses. However, they have not yet been evaluated clinically. Studies have also reported the potential for varying degrees of cross-protection between hantavirus species, although protection remains limited by antigenic diversity. Overall, current evidence supports further development of nucleic acid-based hantavirus vaccines, particularly multivalent strategies, with emphasis on standardized evaluation and clinical efficacy.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, and no specific antivirals exist; licensed vaccines are limited to a few Asian countries.
analysis.main_directions: The review compiles recent DNA and mRNA vaccine advances, emphasizing antigen design, delivery platforms, immunogenicity, safety, and translational progress for HTNV, PUUV, and ANDV.
analysis.current_state: DNA vaccines have demonstrated immunogenicity and acceptable safety in preclinical and early clinical studies, while mRNA vaccines show strong humoral and cellular responses in preclinical models but have not yet entered clinical trials.
analysis.gaps: Cross‑protection is limited by antigenic diversity and mRNA candidates lack clinical evaluation, underscoring the need for standardized efficacy assessments.
analysis.future_research: Future work should prioritize multivalent nucleic‑acid vaccine designs, standardized preclinical and clinical evaluation, and human trials to confirm safety and efficacy across hantavirus species.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause severe disease and lack specific antivirals, with few licensed vaccines. Main directions: The review surveys DNA and mRNA vaccine advances, focusing on antigen design, delivery, immunogenicity, safety, and translational steps for HTNV, PUUV, ANDV. Current state: DNA vaccines are immunogenic and safe in early studies; mRNA vaccines show promising preclinical immunity but no clinical data. Gaps: Antigenic diversity limits cross‑protection and mRNA vaccines lack human trials, requiring standardized efficacy metrics. Future research: Develop multivalent nucleic‑acid vaccines, apply uniform evaluation standards, and conduct clinical trials to establish safety and efficacy.

papers.title_zh: DNA和mRNA疫苗针对汉坦病毒:抗原设计、递送策略与转化进展

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒es 引起 肾综合征出血热 和 汉坦病毒心肺综合征,且暂无特异性抗病毒药物;获批疫苗仅限于少数亚洲国家。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述汇总了近期DNA和mRNA疫苗的进展,重点强调抗原设计、递送平台、免疫原性、安全性以及针对HTNV、PUUV和ANDV的转化进展。
analysis_zh.current_state: DNA疫苗在临床前和早期临床研究中已显示出免疫原性和可接受的安全性;而mRNA疫苗在临床前模型中表现出强烈的体液和细胞免疫应答,但尚未进入临床试验。
analysis_zh.gaps: 由于抗原多样性导致的交叉保护受限,且mRNA候选疫苗缺乏临床评估,凸显了标准化疗效评估的必要性。
analysis_zh.future_research: 未来工作应优先考虑多价核酸疫苗设计、标准化的临床前和临床评估,以及在人类试验中确认对 汉坦病毒 物种的安全性和有效性。

papers.title: Epidemiology and Economic Burden of Puumala Virus Infection in Styria, Austria, 2003 to 2024.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hantavirus infections cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and impose a potential burden on healthcare systems. However, comprehensive economic data remain scarce. We quantified the inpatient economic burden of hospitalized patients with Puumala virus (PUUV) infections in Styria, Austria's primary endemic region, to identify hospitalization costs and early admission predictors of costs. METHODS: This retrospective cost-of-illness study analyzed 1049 serologically confirmed PUUV hospitalizations across 20 public hospitals in Styria, Austria between September 2003 and March 2024. Costs were estimated using the Austrian performance-oriented hospital financing (Leistungsorientierte Krankenanstaltenfinanzierung) diagnosis-related group system, standardized to 2024-equivalent Euros using consumer price index deflation. Admission predictors of cost were assessed using multivariable γ-generalized linear modeling with multiple imputations. Temporal trends in length of stay were analyzed using weighted segmented linear regression. RESULTS: Cumulative inpatient cost was ∼€10.3 million (mean per-case: €9788) for the entire study period of 21 years. Three epidemic years (2012, 2019, and 2021) accounted for 53.6% of cases and over €5.2 million in expenditure, with peak annual costs reaching €1.93 million (0.274% of total Styrian inpatient expenditure) in 2012. Prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT; cost-ratio 1.024 per second, 95% CI 1.019-1.030) and older age (CR 1.004 per year, 95% CI 1.001-1.008) were independent admission-level predictors of higher cost. Median hospital length of stay declined by ∼50% over the study period. CONCLUSIONS: PUUV hospitalizations impose a sharply episodic but recurrent economic burden on regional healthcare systems. Admission aPTT and age independently predicted cost, but clinical outcomes were not modeled and these variables do not constitute a triage tool. Epidemic preparedness strategies are warranted.

analysis.background: Hantavirus infections cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and impose a potential burden on healthcare systems.
analysis.methods: Retrospective cost‑of‑illness study of 1,049 serologically confirmed PUUV hospitalizations across 20 public hospitals in Styria, Austria (Sept 2003–Mar 2024); costs estimated via the Austrian DRG system and standardized to 2024 €; admission cost predictors assessed with multivariable γ‑GLM and multiple imputation; length‑of‑stay trends examined using weighted segmented linear regression.
analysis.results: Cumulative inpatient cost was ≈€10.3 million (mean €9,788 per case) over 21 years; three epidemic years (2012, 2019, 2021) accounted for 53.6 % of cases and >€5.2 million, with a peak annual cost of €1.93 million (0.274 % of Styrian inpatient spending) in 2012; prolonged aPTT (cost‑ratio 1.024 per s, 95 % CI 1.019‑1.030) and older age (CR 1.004 per yr, 95 % CI 1.001‑1.008) independently predicted higher cost; median length of stay declined ~50 % over the period.
analysis.contribution: The study quantifies the episodic but recurrent economic burden of PUUV hospitalizations and identifies admission‑level predictors of cost, informing regional preparedness and resource allocation.
analysis.limitations: Only abstract data are provided, limiting detail on methodology, potential confounders, and broader generalizability.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infections cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and may burden healthcare systems. Methods: Retrospective cost‑of‑illness analysis of 1,049 PUUV hospitalizations in Styria (2003‑2024) using Austrian DRG costing, γ‑GLM for cost predictors, and segmented regression for length‑of‑stay trends. Results: Total inpatient cost ≈€10.3 M (mean €9,788 per case); three epidemic years contributed 53.6 % of cases and >€5.2 M, with a peak annual cost of €1.93 M in 2012; longer aPTT and older age independently increased cost; median stay fell ~50 % over time. Contribution: Provides the first comprehensive economic quantification of PUUV hospitalizations and identifies cost predictors, aiding preparedness. Limitations: Only abstract information is available, restricting methodological detail.

papers.title_zh: 2003至2024年奥地利施蒂利亚地区 普马拉病毒 感染的流行病学与经济负担。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒感染导致肾综合征出血热,并对医疗系统构成潜在负担。
analysis_zh.methods: 回顾性疾病成本研究,涵盖奥地利施蒂利亚州20家公立医院中1,049例血清学确诊的普马拉病毒住院病例(2003年9月–2024年3月);成本通过奥地利DRG系统估算并按2024欧元标准化;使用多变量γ-GLM和多重插补评估入院成本预测因子;采用加权分段线性回归分析住院时长趋势。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究量化了普马拉病毒住院的间歇性但反复出现的经济负担,并识别了入院层面的成本预测因子,为地区防备与资源配置提供依据。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要数据,限制了方法细节、潜在混杂因素及更广泛适用性的阐述。
